catalogTitle: פסוקי דזמרה Destroys The Barriers that Block our תפילה . Explanation of the לשם יחוד Before ברוך שאמר (Intro to פסוקי דזמרה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why later generations need a longer davening, such as Pesukei d'Zimra and the added L'shem Yichud, and what L'shem Yichud means: uniting the hidden and the revealed aspects of Hashem against the concealment of Amalek.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that the Gemara treats Pesukei d'Zimra, like Maariv, as less than a full obligation, yet today it is accepted as one. He compares this to the question put to the Tzemach Tzedek: why are we stricter in kashrus than the Gemara and Rishonim? The answer, from the Tanya, is that food holds sparks of kedushah that eating must extract from the tumah around it; earlier generations were holier and could do this with foods we cannot. In the same way our davening grew longer, and the L'shem Yichud before Baruch She'amar was added. He explains its simple meaning: Hashem is one, but is perceived above as Havaya and below as the Shechinah, and every mitzvah aims to unite them with love and fear. Amalek hides Hashem's presence, which is why His name is hidden in the Megillah. Every mitzvah joins the hidden and the revealed, and a Jew must see Hashem behind the mask.

en: Pesukei d'Zimra, which the Gemara does not treat as a strict obligation, has become an obligation today because Klal Yisrael accepted it.

Food contains sparks of kedushah bound up in tumah, and eating with the Torah's process and with kavanah extracts them; earlier, holier generations could do this with foods later generations cannot, which is why later poskim are stricter.
For the same reason later generations need a longer davening, and the L'shem Yichud before Baruch She'amar was added.

Hashem is absolutely one, but He is perceived above as Havaya and in Klal Yisrael as the Shechinah, read as Adnus; the avodah of every mitzvah is to unite the two, and it needs both love and fear of Hashem.
Amalek works to hide Hashem's presence in this world, so the Megillah, which deals with hester panim, hides Hashem's name, yet His hand shows through at every turning point.
The Rav says a Jew should identify Hashem in every event that happens to him or in the world, and not be blinded by the mask.

title.en: Pesukei d'Zimra becomes an obligation

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Gemara mentions Pesukei d'Zimra but does not seem to make it a strong obligation, yet today it is accepted as one, like Maariv, which the Gemara calls optional. He then introduces the question once put to the Tzemach Tzedek about why later poskim are stricter than the Rishonim.

title.en: Sparks of kedushah in food

summary.en: Answering from the Tanya, the Rav explains that food holds sparks of kedushah bound in tumah: forbidden food cannot be refined, while kosher food can, through shechitah, salting and a brachah with kavanah. The greater the kedushah, as in bread, the greater the tumah around it; earlier generations were holier and could refine foods that later generations must avoid.

title.en: A longer davening and L'shem Yichud

summary.en: The Rav applies the same idea to davening: later generations need a longer tefillah to purify themselves, and parts were added in recent centuries, among them the L'shem Yichud said before Baruch She'amar. He brings Rebbe Elimelech on its power, notes that it is Kabbalah but that every level of Torah also has a pshat, and sets out to explain it simply.

title.en: Uniting Kudsha Brich Hu and the Shechinah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem is absolutely one, but is perceived in different levels: above as the name Havaya, and dwelling in Klal Yisrael as the Shechinah, read as Adnus. All avodah aims to unite the two, and like every mitzvah this needs love and fear of Hashem, the two wings that lift a mitzvah up.

title.en: Yud-Kei, Vav-Kei and Amalek's concealment

summary.en: The Rav explains uniting Yud-Kei, which belongs to the upper world, with Vav-Kei, Hashem's revelation in this world. Amalek is the head of the forces that hide Hashem, which is why the name and throne are incomplete in the war with Amalek, and why the Megillah, set in a time of hester panim, does not mention Hashem's name.

title.en: Hashem masked in the Megillah and in history

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'HaMelech' in the Megillah hints at Hashem, that the Megillah has no open miracles yet its events click together into one great nes, and that Hashem's name hides in the initial and final letters at its turning points. He adds that today too one can see Hashem in history, as everything in the world revolves around Klal Yisrael and Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Mitzvah as Yud-Kei Vav-Kei; removing the mask

summary.en: The Rav shows through the At-Bash letter exchange that the word mitzvah is Yud-Kei, hidden, with Vav-Kei, revealed, so every mitzvah is a yichud. L'shem Yichud is said in the name of all Klal Yisrael, as a declaration to oneself of why one does the mitzvah. He ends with the avodah of Adar: to recognize Hashem in every event and rip off the mask, as on Purim.

oneLiner.en: The Rav tells bachurim that a Jew must rise higher every day, that the day is built by going to sleep on time and waking with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim, and that every act of a Jew affects all of creation and other Jewish souls.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Avraham Avinu, who kept travelling higher, and with the Yid HaKadosh, for whom each day was a new level: a Jew cannot stand still, so each morning must begin fresh. The real preparation for the day is the night before: going to sleep on time, sleeping enough, and lying down with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim and Krias Shema al hamitah, as the opening of the Shulchan Aruch implies. On waking, the first thought, word and act belong to Hashem: Modeh Ani, negel vasser, no snooze button, since everything follows the beginning. He then explains that man is master of creation; in the generation of the Flood even the earth sinned through its owners, while Noach's portion was saved. Every Jew affects other souls of his root, so negel vasser purifies the whole world, and a Jew fighting the yetzer hara is fighting for others too. He ends with the Sanzer Rav and a bachur's excuses for coming late.

en: A Jew can never stand in one place like an angel; he either rises or falls, so each day must be better than the last.
The day really begins the night before: going to sleep on time, sleeping enough, and lying down with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim.
The first thought, the first word and the first act of the morning should be for Hashem, since the whole day follows its beginning.
Man is the master of creation; each Jew has a portion of the world, which is elevated or spoiled by his deeds.
Jews are bound to one another, so a mitzvah such as negel vasser purifies not only the one who does it but other souls of his root and all of creation.

title.en: Rising higher each day, and going to sleep on time

summary.en: The Rav brings Avraham's continual travelling higher and the Yid HaKadosh, for whom each day was a new level, and says a Jew cannot stand still like an angel. He then teaches that the day is prepared the night before: going to sleep on time without idle talk, and sleeping enough to be alert in the shiur.

title.en: Lying down with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim

summary.en: Through Rabbi Meir of Premishlan's reading of the first halacha of the Shulchan Aruch, the Rav explains that one who goes to sleep like a lion rises like a lion. He speaks of Krias Shema al hamitah, which drives away harmful forces, and of the verse in Mishlei about the sluggard, read as a call to go to sleep on time.

title.en: The first thought, word and act of the morning

summary.en: The Rav describes waking with kabbalas ol: Modeh Ani said aloud and with feeling, explained in two ways, and getting up at once without the snooze button. Like a bachur who jumps up early on the day he leaves for camp, a Jew should rise each day for avodas Hashem, dedicating his first thought, speech and deed.

title.en: Man as master of creation; the Flood

summary.en: From Tehillim, that all was placed under man's feet, the Rav explains how in the generation of the Flood even animals and the earth sinned: each person's portion of creation is spoiled by his sins. Noach's portion, including Eretz Yisrael, did not sin and was spared.

title.en: Jews bound together like one body

summary.en: The Rav explains that some Jews, even simple ones with lofty souls, are leaders over hundreds, and that through man's conduct angels, sun and moon praise Hashem better. Like limbs of one body, where an infected finger sickens the whole body, Jews are intermixed, and a mitzvah lights up many souls of one's root, according to the level of one's soul.

title.en: A tzaddik's late candle-lighting; fighting for others

summary.en: The Rav tells of a tzaddik who lit Shabbos candles slightly late and whose truthful student admitted it, and explains that Hashem may let a tzaddik stumble so that his teshuvah arouses others. Each Jew influences those of his root; his negel vasser purifies others too, and when fighting the yetzer hara he should remember that his sin harms other Jews.

title.en: The responsibility of a general

summary.en: The Rav says negel vasser purifies not only the hands but the body and all of creation, and that being a Jew is a responsibility like that of a general whose mistake can lose a war. The first thought, word and deed of the morning are malchus shamayim, and every tefillah and mitzvah acts in the upper and lower worlds.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav and the excuse

summary.en: Speaking of a bachur who comes late with a good excuse, the Rav tells of a man who came to the Sanzer Rav in a new bekishe of old cloth that tore, and of the Sanzer Rav's remark about the face of one who has an excuse. He explains that Heaven helps one who truly wants to come on time, and that a shogeg brings a korban because the excuse itself shows a lack of care.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the mitzvah to speak of Hashem's wonders and then shows them in nature: the measured oxygen in the air, the renewal of the body's cells, the blood and its clotting, and the expansion of matter in heat.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the mitzvah from divrei kabbalah to speak of all of Hashem's wonders, which brings a person to emunah, and with the Ramban in parshas Bo on the passuk about telling one's children. He asks why the chapters of Tehillim that praise Hashem are arranged by the alef-beis, and answers that one can never finish His praises; David ends only because the letters end, as the Gemara shows about the one who added praises in his tefillah. He then sets out to accustom the bachurim to see wonders everywhere. He describes how plants and animals exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide so that the air holds a measured amount of oxygen; how the body's cells are constantly replaced while the brain cells stay, which keeps memory; how the blood feeds the body, carries away waste and clots at a cut; and how matter expands with heat, as in a thermometer and in railway tracks.

en: Speaking of Hashem's wonders is a mitzvah from divrei kabbalah, and it brings a person to emunah.
The chapters of Tehillim that praise Hashem follow the alef-beis because His praises have no end; David stops only because the letters run out.
The Rav wants the bachurim to grow used to seeing that the whole world, every tree, flower and stream, is full of Hashem's wonders.
Plants give off oxygen and animals give off carbon dioxide, and Hashem keeps the air at a measured amount of oxygen, neither too little to breathe nor so much that everything would burn.
The body's cells are constantly replaced, so that every seven years a person has a new body, but the brain cells are not renewed, and so memory lasts.
Hashem placed in the blood of every living creature a substance that seals a cut on contact with air; without it a person would bleed to death from a small cut.

title.en: The mitzvah to speak of Hashem's wonders

summary.en: The Rav brings the mitzvah to speak of Hashem's wonders and the Ramban in parshas Bo, asks why the chapters of praise in Tehillim follow the alef-beis, and answers that His praises never end. He announces that he will speak of wonders in nature so the bachurim grow used to seeing them everywhere.

title.en: Oxygen and the balance of the air

summary.en: The Rav explains that every moving creature needs oxygen while plants, which do not move, need carbon dioxide; plants give off oxygen and animals give off carbon dioxide. Hashem keeps the air at a measured share of oxygen: less would choke all life, more would let a single fire burn the whole world.

title.en: The cells of the body and the brain

summary.en: The Rav describes the tiny cells that make up every living thing and how they are constantly worn out and replaced, so that every seven years a person has a new body, which helps one understand gilgul. Only the brain cells are not renewed, for otherwise a person could not remember beyond seven years; everything is made with a reckoning.

title.en: The blood and how it stops a cut

summary.en: The Rav describes how the blood brings food and oxygen to every part of the body and carries away carbon dioxide like a sanitation system. He then explains the substance in the blood that dries on contact with air and seals a cut; without it the heart would pump out all the blood from the smallest cut.

title.en: Water, heat and expansion

summary.en: The Rav calls water a wondrous thing and first sets out the rule that every material expands when warm and shrinks when cold. He explains a mercury thermometer by this rule and begins to describe railway tracks, where the recording breaks off.

catalogTitle: Every Word a Silver Coin (Intro to פסוקי דזמרה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that every word of Pesukei d'Zimrah is a silver coin to be counted slowly, explains why true tefillah is dveikus that the soul needs as much as Torah, and why such tefillah is so hard in a generation the Satan is fighting for his life.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the teaching that Pesukei d'Zimrah should be said slowly, like a man counting silver coins, and brings the Magen Avraham that it should take half an hour. He describes people who davened for hours: a Chabad chassid in Williamsburg and the upstairs room of the Tzemach Tzedek shul in Yerushalayim, and the Ba'al HaTanya's letter about an hour and a half for Shacharis. Real avodah shebalev is dveikus, so one who has it cannot leave a word. He brings the Gemara that people deride tefillah, then the dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater, and explains that they are brain and heart: the neshamah needs both to live. A sinner's heart is clogged; a passed test brings a good davening. Today tefillah is hard because the Satan, sensing Moshiach, fights with inventions and spiritual contamination. Yet this generation was sent on a shlichus to stay faithful in enemy territory, and he closes with the Shabbos before Tu B'Shvat.

en: Pesukei d'Zimrah should be said slowly, like counting silver coins, since every word is a coin; the Magen Avraham says it should take half an hour.
Avodah shebalev is not just understanding the words but dveikus to Hashem, and one who davens that way davens slowly because he cannot part from each precious word.
The Gemara says tefillah stands at the heights of the world, yet people deride it.
Torah and tefillah are like the brain and the heart: both are vital, and the neshamah needs tefillah as much as it needs Torah to stay alive.
A good tefillah is hard today because the Satan, seeing that Moshiach is near, fights for his life through new inventions and spiritual contamination.
Every person in this generation was placed here on a shlichus to remain faithful to Hashem amid these conditions, and that is what will bring the geulah.

title.en: Every word a silver coin

summary.en: The Rav opens with the teaching that Pesukei d'Zimrah should be said slowly, like a man counting silver coins, and brings the Magen Avraham that it should take half an hour. He explains that Pesukei d'Zimrah is one unit framed by two brachos, and mentions tzaddikim who spent much longer.

title.en: Those who davened all day

summary.en: The Rav recalls a Chabad chassid in Williamsburg who davened Shacharis on Shabbos until the afternoon with tears, the upstairs room of the Tzemach Tzedek shul for those who davened all day, and the Ba'al HaTanya's letter that weekday Shacharis should take at least an hour and a half. He laments that today people mock such davening, and defines avodah shebalev as dveikus.

title.en: Torah or tefillah: which is greater

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who davens with real kavanah cannot leave a word he treasures, and asks why people praise long learning but deride long davening, bringing the Gemara that people make light of tefillah. He then brings the dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater and how it bears on turning a shul into a beis medrash, and explains that the word tefillah means attachment.

title.en: The brain and the heart

summary.en: The Rav compares Torah to the brain and tefillah to the heart: among the 248 limbs some are vital and some not, and since a person cannot live without either, the question which is greater matters only for the halacha. He notes that some tzaddikim davened fast because they were purified, but ordinary people must toil until tefillah touches the heart, and one must merit a good tefillah.

title.en: A clogged heart and the king's daughter

summary.en: The Rav explains that just as the heart's vessels can clog, a sinner's heart is clogged and his davening becomes lip service, while passing a test brings a good davening. He tells the parable of the man who killed a dangerous serpent and won the king's daughter, who is tefillah, and with her access to the King.

title.en: The Satan's last battle: inventions

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the footsteps of Moshiach the Satan, sensing his defeat, fights harder. For thousands of years, from Noach's plow and Adam's fire, there was no progress, and only in the last two hundred years came an explosion of inventions that enslave people, take away their peace and, through the internet, destroy homes. Like a candle that flares before it goes out, this is the Satan fighting for his life.

title.en: A contaminated world, and why we are here

summary.en: The Rav explains that minds and hearts are hampered today because the spiritual atmosphere is contaminated, mirrored by polluted air, water and food, and that the radio shows how every word, of Torah or otherwise, fills the atmosphere. He asks whether we should complain to Hashem, and answers that every neshamah is placed in its time, place and family for a reason, to prove itself despite the conditions.

title.en: The shlichus of our generation

summary.en: The Rav concludes that this generation was chosen for a shlichus no other generation had, like the best soldiers sent to the most dangerous front, to fight the yetzer hara wherever it is and remain faithful, which will bring the geulah. He closes by speaking of the coming Shabbos before Tu B'Shvat as a landmark from which the year climbs toward Purim, Pesach and Shavuos.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the place of Shmuel Hanavi is the place of Rosh Hashanah, since there Chana, who was remembered on Rosh Hashanah, revealed the ways of tefillah and was answered with Shmuel, the first of the prophets.

abstract.en: The Rav suggests that just as each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a mitzvah, the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah: the haftarah of Rosh Hashanah tells of Chana, who conceived Shmuel on the day called 'haras olam'. All the laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, including davening quietly and lengthening one's prayer, which Eli did not know; tefillah, the Rav notes, is something people belittle. He brings a Midrash that reads 'barren' as barren in tefillah and in Torah, and says the place is a segulah for one who struggles to daven or learn. Shmuel's first prophecy punished Chofni and Pinchas for holding back the women's return home. Chana was the first to use the name Tzevakos, praying for children. Finally, citing the Chasam Sofer, he says Chana's prayer in Shiloh was on Rosh Hashanah, and closes with blessings for the coming year.

en: Each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a mitzvah, and the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, alongside the Beis Hamikdash, just as milah has a place both in Chevron and in Shechem.
Rosh Hashanah is 'hayom haras olam', the day the world is conceived anew, and here Chana conceived Shmuel, the first of the prophets, on that very day.
All the laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, among them davening quietly and lengthening one's prayer, both of which Eli did not know.
The place of Shmuel Hanavi is a segulah for one who struggles to daven or to learn, to bring forth fruit from his Torah and tefillah.
Chana was the first in history to call Hashem by the name Tzevakos, and she used it to pray for children.
Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh even on Rosh Hashanah, and it was then that Chana davened and was answered.

summary.en: The Rav says that each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a mitzvah, and suggests that the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, alongside the Beis Hamikdash, as milah has places in both Chevron and Shechem. Rosh Hashanah is 'haras olam', and here Chana conceived Shmuel, the first of the prophets.

title.en: The laws of tefillah learned from Chana

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that many laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, such as standing before the King in Shemoneh Esrei. Eli thought her drunk because he did not know one davens quietly, nor that lengthening one's prayer is a virtue; tefillah, the Rav says, is among the things people belittle.

title.en: Barren in tefillah and Torah: a segulah of the place

summary.en: The Rav mentions that they davened at Shmuel Hanavi that day and that Chana taught long prayer. He brings a Midrash that reads 'barren' as barren in tefillah and Torah, prayer or learning that bears no fruit, and says the place is a segulah for one who struggles to daven or learn.

title.en: Shmuel's first prophecy and the name Tzevakos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shmuel's first prophecy was a punishment on Chofni and Pinchas, whose sin was delaying the women's offerings and so keeping them from home. He then shows that Chana was the first to use the name Tzevakos, which the Chassidic sefarim link to netzach and hod, the source of prophecy, and that she used it to pray for children.

title.en: Chana's prayer was on Rosh Hashanah; blessings

summary.en: The Rav connects 'v'hayah' to the month of Tishrei and brings from the Chasam Sofer that Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh even on Rosh Hashanah, when Chana davened. He concludes that those who came to this place should take on the quality of Rosh Hashanah, of Chana and of Shmuel, and blesses all with a good year.

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches the bachurim that every day and every tefillah is a new creation with its own tikkunim, so the beginning of the day, of davening and of learning must be sanctified, down to a person's first word, thought, sight and even his Jewish name.

abstract.en: The Rav returns to his warning against talking before davening, allowing only kind and holy words, and tells the bachurim to daven slowly and with their yeshiva. He describes davening as an ascent through the worlds of Asiyah, Yetzirah and Beriah up to Shemoneh Esrei before the King, and a descent that brings the shefa down, each step marked by a Kaddish, so parts should not be skipped as a habit. He speaks of the higher Shabbos davening and of a chazzan who must lift the tzibbur, with a story of the Sanzer Rav. Every day, he explains, is a new world with new tikkunim, so a missed tefillah cannot be made up. The beginning carries the whole act, as with writing a Sefer Torah lishmah, learning and davening. Therefore Modeh Ani is said at once, the first sight should be holy, and a Jew should be called by his Jewish name, which holds his shlichus.

en: The Rav says the first words of the day should be words before Hashem, and talking before Shacharis takes away the help from Heaven to daven well.
Davening rises through the worlds up to Shemoneh Esrei and then brings the shefa down; each passage is marked by a Kaddish, so one should not skip parts as a habit.
Every day is a new creation with its own task, so every tefillah does tikkunim that no other tefillah can do, and a missed davening cannot be made up.
The intention stated at the beginning carries through the whole act, as with writing a Sefer Torah, learning and davening, so one should say at the start that he is doing it for the mitzvah.
On waking, the first word, thought, act and sight should be devoted to Hashem: Modeh Ani at once, before washing, and a look at the tzitzis or mezuzah.
Each Jew has his own shlichus, alluded to in his name, so he should be called by his Jewish name, which strengthens his soul, and not by a non-Jewish name, which strengthens the sitra achra.

title.en: No talking before davening

summary.en: The Rav repeats that the first words of the day should be before Hashem and that talking before Shacharis costs the help from Heaven, while allowing short, kind words and holy words that prepare for davening. He tells the bachurim to daven slowly, rise earlier, and daven with their yeshiva as its rules require.

title.en: The worlds of davening and the Kaddeishim

summary.en: The Rav maps davening onto the worlds: korbanos in Asiyah, Pesukei d'Zimrah in Yetzirah, the brachos of Krias Shema in Beriah, and Shemoneh Esrei before the King, then the descent that brings the shefa down, with a Kaddish at each passage. He concludes that although halachah permits a latecomer to skip, by pnimiyus one should not make a habit of it.

title.en: Shabbos davening and the baal tefillah

summary.en: The Rav says coming late on Shabbos loses diamonds, since the Shabbos davening is far higher, and asks those who cannot sing well to daven quietly. A baal tefillah must lift the tzibbur and not rush, as shown by a story of the Sanzer Rav leading a hasty chazzan away from the amud.

title.en: Every day a new world, every tefillah new tikkunim

summary.en: The Rav explains that since creation no day has had the same task, so although the words of davening repeat, their inner kavanos differ, and the words composed with ruach hakodesh effect tikkunim even unknowingly. Each morning one makes a new covenant with Hashem like Adam on his first day, each Krias Shema is a new kabbalas ol, and a lost tefillah cannot be repaired the next day.

title.en: The beginning carries the whole act

summary.en: The Rav brings the halachah that a sofer must say at the start that he writes for the sanctity of the Sefer Torah, and that this beginning holds even when his mind is later absorbed. He applies it to learning, bringing the Tanya on saying it each hour because of the changing combinations of the Name, to davening for the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart, and to living in Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Modeh Ani and the first moments of the day

summary.en: The Rav compares waking to a new birth: just as the yetzer hara comes to a child before the yetzer tov, it rushes in each morning, so Modeh Ani must be said the moment one opens his eyes, which is why it contains no Name of Hashem. The first word, thought, act and sight of the day should be with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim, such as looking at the tzitzis or the mezuzah.

title.en: A Jewish name and its shlichus

summary.en: The Rav teaches that each Jew is sent with his own shlichus, alluded to in his name, bringing Yaakov's question to the angel and Rashi's comment, and suggests combining the letters of one's name with the Name Havayah on waking. He warns against being called by a non-Jewish name, telling of a heretic named Eliezer whose name helped him do teshuvah, and closes by recalling the yahrzeit of Reb Yankele of Pshevorsk.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Jewish emunah rests on the revelation at Har Sinai, witnessed by an entire nation and handed down unchanged, and that the nations' denial of it and their hatred of the Jews come from jealousy of the chosen people, as with Yosef's brothers.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the mesirus nefesh of whole Jewish communities, which goes beyond the trained loyalty of a gentile soldier: Jews carry emunah in the heart. Unlike other faiths, each founded by one individual, Jews believe what an entire nation saw at Har Sinai. Through Rashi's question why the Torah did not begin with 'Hachodesh hazeh lachem', he shows that millions witnessed the revelation, comparing it to undeniable history such as George Washington or Julius Caesar. Every Jew became a prophet, the Sefer Torah was written before eyewitnesses, and every copy is identical. Following the Rambam, belief in Moshe rests on Sinai, so the first mitzvah he taught begins the Torah; and the Torah is eternal, so a prophet who changes it is false. Small differences arose in galus and between the tribes' middos, yet the foundations are shared. The nations deny this from jealousy of the chosen people, as Yosef's brothers did.

en: Jews, even whole cities and communities, gave their lives rather than convert, because emunah is in their heart and not only taught and drilled into them.
Other religions were begun by a single person, while the Jewish faith rests on what a whole nation received at Har Sinai.
An event seen by millions and passed on by a whole people cannot be falsified, just as no one can deny George Washington or Julius Caesar.
Following the Rambam, Jews believe Moshe Rabbeinu because they themselves heard at Sinai Hashem appoint him to teach them the Torah.
The Torah is eternal; no prophet may add to it or take from it, and one who claims Hashem changed a mitzvah is a false prophet.
The foundations of the Torah are the same among all Jews; only small details differ, through forgetting in galus or the tribes' different middos.
The nations hate the Jews out of jealousy, because deep down they know the Jews are the chosen people, as Yosef's brothers were jealous of him.

title.en: Jewish mesirus nefesh for emunah

summary.en: The Rav contrasts a gentile soldier, trained from childhood to die for his country, with Jews who gave their lives rather than convert, even whole communities during the Crusades. He explains that Jews have emunah in the heart, an inheritance from the Avos.

title.en: Faiths founded by one man

summary.en: The Rav explains that every other faith was started by one individual: the founder of Christianity, who made religion easy by permitting forbidden things, and Muhammad, who claimed G-d had changed the Torah. Jews, he says, do not believe one man but what a whole nation received.

title.en: Rashi's question and a nation at Sinai

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's question why the Torah did not begin with 'Hachodesh hazeh lachem', and starts building the answer: millions stood at Har Sinai, heard Hashem and became prophets. A whole people cannot pass on a lie to its children, just as no one can deny George Washington, Julius Caesar or Alexander the Great.

title.en: The Sefer Torah written before witnesses

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew at Sinai was a prophet, and at the end of forty years Moshe wrote the Sefer Torah before people who had seen everything in it; every Jew wrote his own, so all are identical to this day. He brings 'panim b'fanim' and 'ki sh'al na', and notes that Christians and Muslims admit Matan Torah but claim Hashem changed His mind.

title.en: Why we believe Moshe Rabbeinu

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah: Jews believe Moshe because at Sinai they heard Hashem appoint him to teach them the rest of the Torah, after they asked that Moshe speak to them. Therefore, he concludes, the Torah should have begun with 'Hachodesh', the first mitzvah Moshe taught, which answers Rashi's question.

title.en: The Torah is eternal

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that the Torah stands forever, with the pesukim against adding or subtracting, 'the revealed things are ours forever' and 'it is not in heaven'. A prophet cannot change a halachah, so one who says a mitzvah was only for a time, like moving Shabbos to Sunday or Friday, is a false prophet.

title.en: One Torah, small differences

summary.en: The Rav explains that the same Torah passed down through the generations; in galus some details were forgotten and disputes arose, but the foundations are shared by all Jews. Disputes are 'eilu v'eilu': middas chesed and middas din both come from Hashem, each tribe had its own judges, as with Beis Hillel and Beis Shammai, and the tefillin of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam.

title.en: Why the nations deny and hate

summary.en: The Rav asks why the nations, who admit Matan Torah, claim it was changed, and why they hate Jews even today when neither they nor many Jews keep their religion. He answers that they cannot bear that the Jews are the chosen people, and brings this week's sedra: Yosef's brothers saw their father loved him more and hated him from jealousy.

title.en: Announcements and mazel tov

summary.en: After the shiur there are announcements about a minyan for those who have not yet davened Maariv, and mazel tov wishes to a chassan; the rest of the audio is largely unclear.

catalogTitle: ברכת קריאת שמע Elevates us for Our Private Audience with Hashem (שמונה עשרה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows how Krias Shema and its brachos, above all the remembrance of Yetzias Mitzrayim in Emes V'yatziv, lift a person step by step until he stands before the King in Shemoneh Esrei.

abstract.en: The Rav describes davening as an ascent through the four worlds, ending with Shemoneh Esrei, the climax of tefillah, where a Jew returns to the root of his soul, the Avos. He discusses kavanah in the first bracha and urges learning Sefer Bereishis to know the Avos. Krias Shema holds many mitzvos: accepting Hashem's kingship, readiness for mesiras nefesh, and finally remembering Yetzias Mitzrayim, the basis of emunah and the root of every later redemption. In Mitzrayim the Jews also suffered a spiritual exile, a closed heart that could not daven; the Exodus opened their hearts and mouths, so mentioning it at length before Shemoneh Esrei opens ours. In Shemoneh Esrei one stands in thought in the Kodesh HaKodashim, climbing fifteen steps through the fifteen words of Emes V'yatziv, whose eight 'emes' should not be rushed. Finally one stands before Hashem like David HaMelech, as a poor man.

en: Davening ascends through the four worlds, and Shemoneh Esrei is its climax, where one stands before the King and returns to the root of the soul.
Krias Shema contains many mitzvos, including readiness for mesiras nefesh, and is completed only with the remembrance of Yetzias Mitzrayim.
Yetzias Mitzrayim, witnessed by the whole nation, is the basis of emunah and contains the power of every later redemption.
The Exodus freed the Jews from a spiritual exile in which their hearts were closed and they could not daven, so mentioning it before Shemoneh Esrei opens the heart and mouth.
In Shemoneh Esrei a person stands in thought in the Kodesh HaKodashim, and the fifteen words of Emes V'yatziv are fifteen steps up to it.
The eight times 'emes' in Emes V'yatziv should be said slowly and internalized, not rushed.
One should enter Shemoneh Esrei like David HaMelech, as a poor man who has nothing, because the tefillah of the poor man is the strongest.

title.en: Ascending the four worlds to Shemoneh Esrei

summary.en: The Rav explains that creation came down through four worlds, Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, and that davening climbs back up through them to Shemoneh Esrei, the climax of tefillah. Tefillah is the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart, and in it a Jew returns to the root of his soul, Avraham Avinu.

title.en: Kavanah in Avos and knowing the Avos

summary.en: The Rav discusses the requirement of kavanah in the first bracha, why today one does not repeat Shemoneh Esrei without it, and the difference between fulfilling the rabbinic and the Torah mitzvah of tefillah. In a parenthetical remark he urges learning Sefer Bereishis well, since one cannot have kavanah in Avos without knowing the Avos.

title.en: The mitzvos of Krias Shema

summary.en: The Rav lists the mitzvos contained in Krias Shema: readiness for mesiras nefesh, which atones like dying al kiddush Hashem, accepting Hashem's kingship and His oneness, love of Hashem, and finally remembering Yetzias Mitzrayim. He explains that emunah rests on the Exodus that the whole nation witnessed, and that it holds the redemptions of every generation and individual.

title.en: Remembering and elaborating on the Exodus

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk that answers the fear of the nations with 'remember what Hashem did to Pharaoh', and explains that remembering the Exodus is itself a protection. He cites the rule that one who does not say Emes V'yatziv has not fulfilled his obligation, and explains that Emes V'yatziv is where one elaborates on the Exodus and the splitting of the sea.

title.en: The double exile and the opened heart

summary.en: The Rav explains that in Mitzrayim the Jews were in a physical and a spiritual exile: their hearts were closed and they could not daven or feel close to Hashem, like the blockage one sometimes feels in davening. The Exodus opened the gates of tefillah, which is why it is called Pesach, the mouth that speaks, and mentioning it before Shemoneh Esrei opens our hearts and mouths.

title.en: Standing in the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: The Rav explains that in Shemoneh Esrei one should imagine standing in the Beis HaMikdash in the Kodesh HaKodashim, because a person is where his thought is, and he proves this from the halacha of one who sets his Shabbos place by a tree. The fifteen steps up to the Azarah correspond to the fifteen Shir HaMaalos and to fifteen words beginning with vav in Emes V'yatziv.

title.en: Not rushing Emes V'yatziv: the eight 'emes'

summary.en: The Rav laments the habit of rushing Emes V'yatziv and tells of a tzaddik who protested a chazzan's speed with a mashal of meat pulled from a hungry man's mouth. He explains the four times 'emes' after Yetzias Mitzrayim as corresponding to the four exiles, Bavel, Paras, Yavan and Edom, and another four that reinforce them, eight in all, which one should say slowly and absorb.

title.en: Approaching the King as a poor man

summary.en: The Rav describes how David HaMelech, who had everything, saw himself as a poor man with nothing, and how such a request is granted. He brings three kinds of tefillah, of Moshe (contemplation of Hashem's greatness), of David (song and joy) and of the poor man (a broken heart), the last being the strongest, and concludes that before Shemoneh Esrei we take on David HaMelech's stance as poor men.

oneLiner.en: Through stories of tzaddikim, the Rav shows the bachurim how great people went out of their way never to trouble or pain another Jew, even at a cost to themselves or to a mitzvah.

abstract.en: The Rav tells the bachurim that this time he wants to speak about middos, and to do it through stories of tzaddikim. He tells how Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld asked each Yom Tov visitor whether he had been at the Kosel, so that a guest sitting with him would not feel slighted, and how he moved back to the Old City before his passing so that the Jews at his levayah would not have to walk far. He gave the Rosh Hashanah musaf to the son of the late chazzan for the widow's sake. The Chofetz Chaim skipped the na'anuim on the town's only esrog so as not to pain those who had none. Rav Moshe Kliers declared a broken eruv kosher to protect the honor of the Sefardi chacham, and Rav Chaim Ozer weighed a servant's trouble and kept a guest company in the sukkah. After taking leave of the bachurim for several weeks, the Rav ends with the Chofetz Chaim's rebuke of talmidim who laughed at a broken-hearted woman, and Rav Elchonon Wasserman's seriousness.

en: The Rav says he is speaking to the bachurim about middos this time, through stories of how tzaddikim served Hashem.
Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld returned to the Old City before his passing against his doctors' advice, so that Jews would not have to walk far to his burial on Har HaZeisim.
Rav Yosef Chaim had the son of the late baal musaf lead musaf on Rosh Hashanah, so that the widow would not suffer hearing a stranger in her husband's place.
The Chofetz Chaim did not shake the only esrog in town during Hallel, so as not to cause pain to everyone who could not do so.
Rav Moshe Kliers explained that he called a broken eruv kosher because the honor of the Torah, embodied in the Sefardi chacham, outweighed an issur derabbanan.

Rav Chaim Ozer considered the trouble of his household servant before taking a summer apartment, and, though exempt from sukkah, came down to keep a poor guest company because he was not exempt from hachnasas orchim.
The Chofetz Chaim sharply rebuked talmidim who laughed at a simple woman's words, saying one may not laugh at a person with a heavy heart.

title.en: Middos through stories; the visitors and the Kosel

summary.en: The Rav says he will speak about middos through stories of tzaddikim. He tells how Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld asked each Yom Tov visitor whether he had been at the Kosel, so that the Lubliner Rav sitting with him would not feel slighted.

title.en: Returning to the Old City before his passing

summary.en: Rav Yosef Chaim, sent by his doctors to the airier New City, moved back to the crowded Old City a few weeks before his passing. He explained that his burial would be on Har HaZeisim, and he did not want everyone to walk a long way from the New City.

title.en: The mourner who led musaf on Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: When the baal musaf died days before Rosh Hashanah, Rav Yosef Chaim delayed the choice and then sent the deceased's son to the amud. Asked about the Shulchan Aruch's rule on a mourner leading the davening, he said the widow in the ezras nashim would otherwise suffer, and the Rav calls this the thinking of a tzaddik.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's esrog without na'anuim

summary.en: During the First World War there was one esrog in Radin, brought for the Chofetz Chaim, and everyone made the brachah on it. At Hallel he did not shake it, explaining that the others could fulfil the mitzvah of taking it but could not do na'anuim, and he would not cause them pain.

title.en: The eruv in Teveria and the chacham's honor

summary.en: In Teveria the Sefardi chacham oversaw the eruv. When it broke on Shabbos, Rav Moshe Kliers declared it kosher; after Shabbos the Gemara showed it was pasul. Asked privately, he explained that announcing it would have shamed the chacham and the honor of the Torah, which outweighs an issur derabbanan.

title.en: Rav Chaim Ozer: the servant and the guest in the sukkah

summary.en: Rav Chaim Ozer hesitated to take a spacious summer apartment until the servant agreed, since its kitchen was far from the dining room. Later, ill and exempt from sukkah, he sent a poor guest to eat in the sukkah and came down to sit with him, citing Avraham Avinu's hachnasas orchim.

title.en: Taking leave of the bachurim

summary.en: The Rav tells the bachurim that his doctors are urging him to spend several weeks in Miami for his health, so they will not meet for about four weeks. He says he will miss the davening here and asks that he return with better health.

title.en: Not laughing at a heavy heart

summary.en: A simple woman told the Chofetz Chaim she could not pray at her parents' graves because they were alive; the talmidim laughed and he rebuked them sharply. The Rav adds that Rav Elchonon Wasserman, following Chazal on laughter in this world, was never seen smiling except once, and closes with a l'chaim.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Rav speaks of the preciousness of Eretz Yisroel and warns that one who lives there must keep renewing his appreciation and be truly planted in the land through Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with a Jew who comes from outside the land and merits to live in Eretz Yisroel, the good land the Torah praises as a land of streams of water. The danger, he says, is that one grows used to it, so a person needs constant renewal and must work for it. One indirect way is through davening: when a person concentrates in Pesukei d'Zimra on the praises of Yerushalayim, and on the blessing for Yerushalayim in Shemoneh Esrei. A Jew in Boro Park says these words, but feels far away; a Jew in the land feels close, and must thank Hashem. Citing the week's sedra about settling the land, the Rav says one must rejoice in Eretz Yisroel. He then compares a log laid on the ground, which only rots, to a planted tree that grows: being in the land is not enough, one must be planted in it with the Torah of Eretz Yisroel.

en: A person living in Eretz Yisroel can grow used to it, so he needs constant renewal and must work for it.
One indirect way to renew this feeling is through davening, by concentrating on the praises of Yerushalayim in Pesukei d'Zimra and in Shemoneh Esrei.
A Jew abroad says the same words about Yerushalayim but feels far, while one in the land feels close and must thank Hashem.
Being in Eretz Yisroel is not enough; like a planted tree rather than a log on the ground, one must be planted there through Torah.

title.en: The preciousness of Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav speaks of a Jew who merits to live in Eretz Yisroel, warns against growing used to it, and suggests renewing the feeling through the praises of Yerushalayim in davening. He ends with the parable of a log versus a planted tree: one must be rooted in the land through Torah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Nissan and Pesach are the time of renewal and the 'point' of beginning, the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu and of emunah, and that the matzah is filled with holy Names of emunah and redemption.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Parshas HaChodesh: Nissan is the month of renewal, when the Jewish people became a nation and, according to the halachah, the world was created. Nature itself comes back to life in Nissan; the birds return and fill the air with song, and he explains why morning is called tzafra and night ramsha. Among the three Regalim, Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, yet only Pesach carries kares, because Pesach is the 'point', the beginning and the bond with Hashem, like Avraham Avinu, after whom the first blessing is named Magen Avraham. Pesach is the time to daven and say Hallel with freshness, and a kind of techiyas hamesim. It is the Yom Tov of emunah: matzah is the 'food of faith', filled with holy Names of emunah and geulah. He closes with the gematria of lechem and matzah and a call to keep Pesach with kedushah and care.

en: Nissan is the time of renewal: the Jewish people became a nation then, and the world itself was created in Nissan.
Shavuos and Sukkos are higher Yamim Tovim than Pesach, but Pesach is the 'point' and the beginning, the bond with Hashem, which is why only Pesach carries kares.
Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, and the time of emunah, the point in a Jew's heart on which all mitzvos rest.
On Pesach one must be fresh: daven, say Hallel and the Haggadah with freshness and joy, and rise as in a techiyas hamesim.
The essence of the matzah is the holy Names within it, Names of emunah and of geulah; the baked matzah is only their envelope.

title.en: Nissan, the month of renewal

summary.en: The Rav opens with Parshas HaChodesh and explains that in Nissan the Jewish people became a nation. He brings the dispute whether the world was created in Nissan or Tishrei, Tosafos' resolution, and that the Avos were born in Nissan, so Nissan is the time for a Jew to renew himself.

title.en: Nature comes back to life

summary.en: The Rav describes how the dead winter fields and trees revive in Nissan and the birds return and sing. He explains why morning is called tzafra and night ramsha, says a Jew sings to Hashem at all times, and brings Shir HaShirim on the passing of the winter.

title.en: Pesach, the point of beginning

summary.en: The Rav compares the three Regalim: Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, as seen from Hallel, yet Pesach is the beginning, like Avraham among the Avos. Only Pesach carries kares, the opposite of the bond with Hashem that Pesach makes, and this is why the blessing is Magen Avraham; emunah is the point on which all mitzvos rest.

title.en: Milah, korban Pesach and Avraham

summary.en: The Rav points out that the only two positive mitzvos with kares, milah and the korban Pesach, are both tied to Avraham Avinu, and that Avraham's great events happened on Pesach. Pesach is the bond with Hashem, like a chuppah, while the other Yamim Tovim hold higher things.

title.en: Freshness and techiyas hamesim

summary.en: The Rav says on Pesach one must daven, say Hallel and the Haggadah freshly, bringing the passuk in Eichah and the Targum that the 'mo'ed' there is Pesach. The revival of nature is a techiyas hamesim; he brings the haftorah of Yechezkel's dry bones and says every Jew must rise anew on Pesach.

title.en: Everything is new on Pesach

summary.en: The Rav shows that the whole Yom Tov is built on renewal: new clothes, a painted house, dishes not seen for twelve months. Pesach is the time of emunah, and he brings the Yismach Yisrael that at the seder one plants emunah in the children by telling them of yetzias Mitzrayim.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Rav ties the mitzvah of emunah to Avraham, the first believer, and discusses the nusach 'Ha lachma anya' versus 'Kehah lachma anya'. He brings the Zohar that matzah is the food of faith, as the Jews left Egypt with only matzah, and says the matzah is full of holy Names.

title.en: The holy Names inside the matzah

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Divrei Chaim after the seder and gives the mashal of an esrog that is a plain citrus fruit all year and a holy object on Sukkos. So too the essence of the matzah is the Names of geulah within it, the same as in Egypt; he then tells the bachurim to help at home, learn hilchos Pesach and burn their chametz.

title.en: Lechem and matzah in gematria

summary.en: The Rav shows that lechem equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times that Name spelled out in full, a higher level of holy Names. He closes with a warning to keep Pesach with care and kedushah, since Pesach is emunah, the most important thing a Jew has.

catalogTitle: The Accomplishments of תפילה are Different each Day

oneLiner.en: Starting from facing the Beis HaMikdash in tefillah, the Rav teaches that a person is where his thoughts are, and that a Yid should seek to give Hashem nachas ruach beyond what he is commanded, with tevilas Ezra, mikvah and Rabbeinu Tam tefillin as examples.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shlomo's tefillah that prayers in exile be directed toward the Beis HaMikdash, explains how to face Eretz Yisrael from Borough Park, and says one should have in mind standing in the Kodesh HaKodashim. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is, and the Satmar Rav's proof from the techum Shabbos case of a traveler who fixes his eyes on a tree. Turning to Ezra's takanah of tevilah before learning and davening, he brings his rebbe Reb Shraga Feivel and the Mesilas Yesharim: a loving servant or child does what pleases his master even unasked. He contrasts Bilam with Avraham at the Akeidah, then shows Hashem desires taharah: the Rambam's letter, the Kohen Gadol's tevilos, mikvah before Shabbos. A story of Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, Rabbeinu Tam tefillin and the shofar sounds illustrate the theme, ending with the Rambam on bodily purity bringing purity of soul.

en: When davening, a person should face toward Eretz Yisrael and have in mind that he is standing in the Beis HaMikdash, before the Kodesh HaKodashim.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, a person is located where his thought is, so thoughts of Torah place him in Gan Eden and forbidden thoughts in Gehinnom.
A loving servant or child does not only what he is told but what he knows will please his master or parent; so should a Yid act toward Hashem.
Although Ezra's takanah of tevilah became void, Hashem's desire for avodah in taharah remains, making mikvah a midas chassidus.
Customs such as Rabbeinu Tam tefillin are not an obligation but an extra nachas ruach for Hashem.

title.en: Facing the Beis HaMikdash in tefillah

summary.en: The Rav cites Shlomo's prayer that tefillos in exile be directed toward the Beis HaMikdash, explains how to face Eretz Yisrael from Borough Park, and says to have in mind standing before the Kodesh HaKodashim. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is.

title.en: The Satmar Rav's proof from techum Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Satmar Rav's support for the Ba'al Shem Tov from the din of a traveler far from the city at nightfall who fixes his eyes on a tree and makes it his place. He concludes that one must guard his thoughts, and that one who fixes his mind on the Beis HaMikdash is truly there.

title.en: Ezra's takanah and doing Hashem's will

summary.en: The Rav describes Ezra's takanah requiring tevilah after keri before learning and davening, which did not take hold and became void. He then brings his rebbe Reb Shraga Feivel and the Mesilas Yesharim: a servant or child who loves does what pleases his master unasked, and contrasts Bilam, who tried again and again to bend Hashem's will to his own.

title.en: Avraham at the Akeidah

summary.en: The Rav describes how Avraham, despite Hashem's promise that the Jewish nation would come from Yitzchak, did not argue or daven to change the decree but went to the Akeidah with simcha, keeping pace with Yitzchak as Rashi explains. He returns to the Mesilas Yesharim's image of the devoted son.

title.en: Hashem desires avodah in taharah

summary.en: Reb Shraga Feivel applied this to tevilas Ezra: the requirement of taharah in the Mikdash shows Hashem favors avodah in purity, so though the takanah is void, mikvah is a midas chassidus. The Rav brings the Rambam's letter that he himself kept it though he could not rule it as halachah, the Kohen Gadol's tevilos on Yom Kippur, and mikvah before Shabbos and on Shabbos morning per the Arizal.

title.en: Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and the mikvah

summary.en: The Rav tells how Reb Isser Zalman Meltzer saw Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld leaving the mikvah and asked about the lost learning time; he answered that if a mikvah can make a ger into a Yid, it can make a Yid into a better Yid. The Rav stresses he is not ruling that one must go daily, only that a Yid should seek to give Hashem nachas ruach, like a child bringing his mother a gift.

title.en: Rabbeinu Tam tefillin and the shofar

summary.en: The Rav explains the custom of wearing Rabbeinu Tam tefillin after marriage: the dispute goes back to two ancient practices, the halachah follows Rashi, but the Zohar says both are needed, and starting after the chasunah follows the Gemara's view that one can then learn in purity. He compares the shofar sounds, where the Zohar says both shevarim and teruos are needed, and closes with the Rambam that purity of body brings purity of soul.

oneLiner.en: Before starting to learn Tanya with the bachurim, the Rav traces how the secrets of the Torah came down to the Ba'al Shem Tov's way of avodah, explains what makes the Tanya and its author unique, and tells stories of the Ba'al HaTanya's imprisonment.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the four levels of Torah given at Sinai, pshat, remez, drush and sod, and explains that the secrets were passed only to the greatest students, until Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wrote the Zohar and the Arizal revealed more. The Ba'al Shem Tov taught how to use these secrets for avodas Hashem, and the Maggid's students wrote sefarim on the weekly sedra. The Tanya is different: it builds its subject in order, chapter after chapter, so it opens the other chassidic sefarim. He brings the Satmar Rav's advice to learn Tanya in order to come to want to serve Hashem, describes the Ba'al HaTanya's lofty soul and his Shulchan Aruch, in which every word is weighed, and tells stories of his arrest and interrogation. He closes by announcing that the Tanya shiur will begin next Tuesday.

en: The secrets of the Torah were given at Sinai but passed only to the greatest students, until the Zohar and the Arizal's writings put them in sefarim.
The Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching is to use the secrets of the Torah for avodas Hashem, and his students' sefarim show how.
Unlike the other sefarim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's students, which follow the sedra, the Tanya builds its subject in order, each chapter continuing the one before.
The Tanya teaches how to serve Hashem and is also the key to understanding the other chassidic sefarim, such as the Meor Einayim and the Kedushas Levi.
In the Ba'al HaTanya's works, the Tanya and his Shulchan Aruch, every word and even every letter is measured and weighed.

title.en: The secrets of the Torah and their transmission

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah was given with four levels, pardes, and that its secrets were handed down only to the greatest students. After the Churban, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wrote the Zohar, and later the Arizal revealed new secrets with permission from Heaven.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and his students' sefarim

summary.en: The Rav describes how the Ba'al Shem Tov took the secrets of the Zohar and the Arizal and used them for avodas Hashem, and lists the sefarim of the Maggid and his students. He explains that most tzaddikim did not write their own teachings, and tells how the Meor Einayim let only the teachings he did not remember be written down.

title.en: Why the Tanya is different

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Tanya, unlike the other chassidic sefarim, is a structured work that builds chapter by chapter. He notes that some Rebbes held it reveals too much, but brings the Bnei Yissaschar, the Satmar Rav's advice to learn Tanya in order to want to serve Hashem, and Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz learning it in Torah Vodaath.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya and his Shulchan Aruch

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Tanya opens up the other chassidic sefarim, describes the Ba'al HaTanya as a soul from the world of Atzilus and a great chacham, and tells how the Maggid had him write a Shulchan Aruch, telling him to rewrite its first chapters simply, without sodos.

title.en: Every word weighed: the Shulchan Aruch HaRav

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Ba'al HaTanya deliberating for weeks over one vav in the Tanya, explains why chassidim call him 'the Rav', and brings Reb Yaakov Kamenetsky and Reb Meir Arik on the weight of the Shulchan Aruch HaRav. He adds that it is one of the best ways to understand the Gemara.

title.en: Stories of the Ba'al HaTanya's arrest

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Czar arrested the Ba'al HaTanya, visited him in disguise and tested his wisdom, how he avoided a hidden pit on the way to the judge, and how he had the boat stopped for kiddush levanah by natural means. He ends with the judge's last question about the Tanya, which the Ba'al HaTanya answered only with a smile.

title.en: Starting to learn Tanya together

summary.en: The Rav announces that he will learn Tanya with the bachurim, as he did several times in Torah Vodaath with their fathers, the founders of Emunas Yisroel, who gained much from it. He says it will go slowly and open new understanding of Torah and avodas Hashem, recalls the Ba'al Shem Tov's words about Moshiach, and sets the start for next Tuesday.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Rav teaches that whoever defeats the 'snake' of the yetzer hara receives the 'king's daughter' of tefillah, and that the unprecedented tests of this generation signal how great the reward will be.

abstract.en: The Rav brings the saying that whoever kills the snake is given the king's daughter, and explains that the snake is the yetzer hara and the king's daughter is tefillah. One who overcomes the yetzer hara merits real tefillah, which not everyone merits; it needs preparation. He then says that the tests of today are enormous: with all the new devices and tools that keep coming, this generation faces tests that earlier generations never had. Still, one must work hard against the yetzer hara, not give in, and ask Hashem for help. The very size of these tests, he says, is a sign that what will be received is very great. He mentions a new form of Torah, its inner dimension, that is being revealed, and says one must rejoice, since the tests can be fought and Hashem will help.

en: Whoever kills the 'snake' receives the 'king's daughter': the snake is the yetzer hara and the king's daughter is tefillah.
Not everyone merits true tefillah; it requires preparation.
The tests of this generation, brought by the many new devices, are enormous and were never faced by earlier generations.
One must work hard against the yetzer hara, not give in, and ask Hashem for help.

summary.en: The Rav explains the saying about killing the snake and receiving the king's daughter as overcoming the yetzer hara to merit tefillah. oneLiner.en: Opening a new series for bachurim on tefillah, the Rav explains why he speaks so much about prayer, tells how his beis medrash grew out of a group of bachurim who wanted to daven properly, and shows that the heart of tefillah is kavanah, the awareness of standing before the King.

abstract.en: The Rav announces a new series on tefillah and explains why he speaks about prayer more than Torah: the bachurim hear about Torah all week in yeshiva, while tefillah, as the Gemara says, stands at the heights of the world yet people belittle it. He tells how a group of bachurim he led in a summer camp's masmidim division learned to daven slowly, then asked for a year-round minyan; despite mockery it grew into his beis medrash, whose foundation is tefillah. He brings the Gemara's dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater and the Rambam's ruling. He then teaches that tefillah is the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart, that the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah fixed three daily tefillos, corresponding to the Avos or the korbanos, and that as thought can disqualify a korban, thought and kavanah are the core of tefillah. He closes on the first berachah, standing before the King, and kiddush levanah.

en: The Rav speaks constantly about tefillah because yeshivos speak about Torah all week, while tefillah, though it stands at the heights of the world, is belittled by people.
His beis medrash was built only because bachurim who learned well also wanted to daven well, so its foundation is tefillah.
Tefillah fulfills the mitzvah of serving Hashem with all one's heart, and therefore its core is the heart and the thought.
The Anshei Knesses Hagedolah fixed three daily tefillos, corresponding either to the Avos or to the korbanos.
Since thought alone can invalidate a korban, and tefillah corresponds to the korbanos, thought and kavanah are the essence of tefillah.
Everything before Shemoneh Esrei is preparation, so that a person can stand in prayer feeling that he stands before the King.

title.en: A beis medrash founded on tefillah

summary.en: The Rav describes the beis medrash today and why the early years' davening was better, then explains that it was built for tefillah. He brings the Gemara's dispute whether Torah or tefillah is greater and the Rambam's ruling, and announces the new series on tefillah.

title.en: Service of the heart and the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah

summary.en: The Rav explains that tefillah is the mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart and shows where it appears in kriyas shema. He then describes the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah, who, when prophecy ended in the second Beis Hamikdash, strengthened Yiddishkeit with the rabbinic takanos.

title.en: Three tefillos and the power of thought

summary.en: The Rav brings the two views on whether the three tefillos correspond to the Avos or to the korbanos, and argues that since thought can invalidate a korban, thought is the core of tefillah. Without kavanah one fulfills only the rabbinic obligation, and one must ask Hashem for the kavanah itself.

title.en: Standing before the King; kiddush levanah

summary.en: The Rav discusses kavanah in the first berachah and why the Acharonim say not to repeat Shemoneh Esrei, asks why kavanah should not be needed in all the berachos, and explains that the whole tefillah prepares one to feel he stands before the King. He ends on kiddush levanah as greeting the Shechinah.

catalogTitle: Why is it So Difficult to Daven in these Pre-Moshiach Times?

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that in the last days before Moshiach the Satan fights with new weapons against Hashem and Moshiach, and that tefillah, which is always an act of emunah, is what carries Klal Yisroel through.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chofetz Chaim's statement that we live in ikvesa d'Meshicha, and argues with a coin analogy that every day there is a real chance Moshiach comes, despite all the years of waiting. He distinguishes the fixed ketz, known only to Hashem, from earlier moments when Moshiach could come, and recounts dates predicted by tzaddikim that turned into catastrophes, explaining that at such moments the Satan comes as accuser. The Gemara recorded a passed date to teach that disappointment must not shake emunah; Achashverosh and Daniel miscalculated, and even Rabbi Akiva was wrong about Bar Kochba. He then describes the signs of the footsteps of Moshiach: chutzpah, wrongdoing made lawful, inventions that destroy families, all weapons of the Satan fighting for his life. Against this, tefillah, though mocked, is always lishmah, since turning to Hashem is pure emunah, and emunah will bring the geulah.

en: Every day there is a real chance that Moshiach will come, no matter how long the wait has been.
Only Hashem knows the fixed time of Moshiach; dates predicted by tzaddikim passed and even turned into catastrophes.
A disappointment over a predicted date must not affect one's emunah; this is why the Gemara recorded a date that had already passed.
The signs of the generation before Moshiach are evident today: chutzpah, wrongdoing made lawful, and the breakdown of the family.
The Satan, fighting for his life before Moshiach, brings new inventions as weapons against Hashem and Moshiach.
Tefillah is mocked more than Torah, yet every tefillah is an exercise in emunah, and emunah is what will bring the geulah.

title.en: Moshiach could come any day

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Chofetz Chaim's words that we live in ikvesa d'Meshicha and the Rambam's principle of belief in Moshiach, and uses a spinning coin to show that every day there is an even chance Moshiach comes. He adds that the fixed time of the geulah is known only to Hashem.

title.en: Predicted dates that became catastrophes

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes the fixed ketz from times when Moshiach could be hastened, as in Mitzrayim, and lists dates tzaddikim gave: the Toldos Yaakov Yosef's Tav Shin, the year Tach, the Malbim's 1914, each of which brought catastrophe. He explains that at such a moment the Satan comes as accuser and brings up Klal Yisroel's sins.

title.en: Why the Gemara recorded a date that passed

summary.en: The Rav asks why Ravina and Rav Ashi wrote a date for Moshiach that had already passed, and answers that it teaches not to let disappointment affect emunah. He then brings the Gemara in Megillah that Achashverosh, and even Daniel, miscalculated the seventy years.

title.en: Bar Kochba and the signs of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Rambam, who writes halachos, tells the story of Ben Koziva whom Rabbi Akiva endorsed, and answers that it is itself a lesson: even Rabbi Akiva can be wrong about Moshiach. He then turns to the Gemara's signs of the footsteps of Moshiach, chutzpah and wrongdoing that has become lawful.

title.en: New inventions as the Satan's weapons

summary.en: The Rav contrasts thousands of years of plow and sword with today's explosion of inventions, and explains that worse than weapons that could destroy the world are weapons against Hashem and Moshiach, as in the passuk about tearing off the bonds. The Satan, fighting for his life, uses them to destroy families and shalom bayis.

title.en: The backbone that carries Torah to Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the promise that Torah will not be forgotten and Rabbi Yaakov Emden's words that Jewish survival in golus is a greater miracle than the splitting of the sea. A small backbone of Jews who keep Torah will carry over to the days of Moshiach, and he says they must thank Hashem and put in extra effort now.

title.en: Tefillah is mocked, yet it builds emunah

summary.en: The Rav says tefillah especially is derided today, citing the Gemara that people scorn things that stand at the height of the world, while even one who does not learn still respects Torah. He explains that tefillah fosters emunah, and contrasts Torah learned shelo lishmah, which is justified only because it leads to lishmah.

title.en: A kvitel for a bicycle and a dog

summary.en: The Rav tells of a kvitel at the Kosel in which a boy asked Hashem for a bicycle and a dog, and explains that the very act of turning to Hashem is lishmah and pure emunah, so every tefillah fortifies emunah. He closes with the Gemara that Chabakuk based everything on emunah, and that just as emunah preceded the song at the sea, emunah will bring the song of the geulah.

oneLiner.en: Opening the Tanya for bachurim, the Rav explains why the sefer begins with the word 'Tanya', what the oath 'be a tzaddik and not a rasha' means and why it gives strength, and how the Raya Mehemna reads the four types of people in the Gemara.

abstract.en: The Rav begins the Tanya with the Gemara in Niddah that a soul is sworn before birth to be a tzaddik and not a rasha. He brings the Chabad tradition that the opening word 'Tanya' breaks a kelipah of that name, and that the introduction addresses every Jew in every generation. Citing the Satmar Rebbe, he calls Tanya the sefer for one who wants to want to be good, and reads its letters as the future-tense prefixes. He describes the sefer's order: questions, knowledge, then avodah. He derives shevuah from sheva, the seven forces of creation, so the oath strengthens a person against the yetzer hara, as with Eliezer, and reads 'mashbi'in' as 'mashpi'in'. He then raises the Tanya's question about seeing oneself as a rasha, brings the Gemara's four types with the Raya Mehemna's reading, and ends with beinonim, Rabbah and Iyov.

en: Before a soul comes down it is sworn to be a tzaddik and not a rasha, and even if the whole world calls it a tzaddik it should be in its own eyes like a rasha.
The Tanya is a sefer in avodas Hashem for someone who wants to become better, and the Rav says it answers every question one can ask in avodas Hashem.
The Tanya is built in order: questions in the first chapter, then about ten or fifteen chapters of knowledge, and only then guidance in avodah, which can be understood only with that knowledge.
An oath carries the power of all seven forces of creation and so strengthens a person against the yetzer hara.
According to the Raya Mehemna, a 'tzaddik who has bad' is a tzaddik whose evil is subordinate to him, and a 'rasha who has good' is one who has a yetzer tov but does not obey it.

title.en: Why the sefer opens with 'Tanya'

title.en: A sefer for one who wants to become better

summary.en: The Rav explains that the introduction addresses every Jew in every generation who learns the sefer, brings the Satmar Rebbe's answer that one who wants to want should learn Tanya, and says the sefer answers every question in avodas Hashem. He then reads the four letters of 'Tanya' as the prefixes of the future tense.

title.en: The oath and the order of the Tanya

summary.en: The Rav explains the oath the soul takes, to be a tzaddik and not a rasha and to be like a rasha in its own eyes, and describes the Tanya's system: questions, then knowledge, then avodah. He says he will learn the first chapter with its questions closely and may summarize some later chapters.

title.en: Shevuah, sheva and shefa

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that shevuah comes from sheva: an oath binds a person with all seven forces of creation, which is why one may swear to strengthen himself against the yetzer hara, as Avraham made Eliezer swear. He then reads 'mashbi'in' as 'mashpi'in', since pei and beis interchange and a pei in ksav ashuri holds a hidden beis.

title.en: How can one consider himself a rasha?

summary.en: The Rav raises the Tanya's question: one who sees himself as a rasha will become sad and cannot serve Hashem with simcha, yet one who is always joyful may come to lightheadedness. He explains that 'like a rasha' means not being sure of oneself, and introduces the Gemara in Berachos on four kinds of people.

title.en: The Raya Mehemna on the four types

summary.en: The Rav gives the simple meaning of tzaddik and rasha who fare well or badly, and then the Raya Mehemna in parshas Mishpatim: every person has a yetzer tov and a yetzer hara, and 'tzaddik vera lo' is a tzaddik who masters his evil, while 'rasha vetov lo' has a yetzer tov he does not obey.

title.en: Beinonim, Rabbah and Iyov

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara at the end of Berachos that tzaddikim are judged by the yetzer tov, reshaim by the yetzer hara and beinonim by both, Rabbah's saying that he is a beinoni and Abaye's reply. He then sets out the Tanya's questions: how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim when that is not decreed at birth, and how Rabbah, who never stopped learning, could err in calling himself a beinoni.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Rav explains that the second week of consolation, Parshas Eikev, is a consolation of yiras Shamayim, and that Shabbos is a wellspring of yiras Shamayim.

abstract.en: The Rav explains that the seven weeks of consolation follow the middos. The first week is a consolation of chessed, with its double 'nachamu'. The second week, Parshas Eikev, is a consolation of yirah, fear of Heaven, and indeed the Torah's passage on yirah is read in Eikev. Just as the first week has the reading of Shema with its love, the second has yirah. He connects this to Shabbos, noting that the word Bereishis holds the letters of 'yarei Shabbos': Shabbos gives yiras Shamayim. The consolation of this week is strengthening in yiras Shamayim, which many people greatly need; with today's yetzer hara in the street, guarding oneself is yiras Shamayim, and one should feel joy in it. The haftarah too speaks of those who fear Hashem. He calls Shabbos a wellspring of yiras Shamayim, and closes recalling Rav Shimon of Amshinov, a Jew of great yiras Shamayim.

en: The seven weeks of consolation follow the middos: the first is chessed, the second, Eikev, is yirah.
The consolation of Eikev is strengthening oneself in yiras Shamayim, which many people greatly need.
With today's yetzer hara in the street, guarding oneself is itself yiras Shamayim, and one should feel joy in it.
Shabbos is a wellspring of yiras Shamayim; on Shabbos one draws yiras Shamayim.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a person is where his thoughts are, and that a Yid who wants to give Hashem nachas will seek purity in his tefillah and service even where it is not strictly required.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shlomo HaMelech's tefillah that exiled Jews should turn toward Eretz Yisrael and the Beis Hamikdash, and explains how one in Boro Park should face, and above all have in mind that he stands in the Beis Hamikdash. He grounds this in the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a person is where his thought is, which the Satmar Rav supported from the Gemara about a traveler who fixes his Shabbos place by a tree. He then turns to Ezra's takanah requiring immersion before davening, which was not accepted, and, through his rebbe's teaching from Mesillas Yesharim, contrasts Bilaam, who pressed Hashem to do his will, with Avraham Avinu, who went joyfully to the Akeidah. Hashem favors taharah, as seen in the Kohanim, the Rambam's own practice, the Kohen Gadol's immersions and immersion before Shabbos. A story of Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, Rabbeinu Tam tefillin and the shofar sounds illustrate doing more than the minimum.

en: When davening one should face Eretz Yisrael and, above all, have in mind that one is standing in the Beis Hamikdash, and this is accepted as if one were there.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav teaches that a person is where his thought is: thinking of Torah places him in Gan Eden, and improper thoughts place him in Gehinnom.
Like a devoted child, a Yid should seek to do what gives Hashem pleasure even when he is not commanded, unlike Bilaam who tried to bend Hashem to his own will.
Although Ezra's takanah to immerse before davening was not upheld, Hashem favors service done in taharah, so immersion remains a midas chassidus.
A mikvah adds kedushah even to one who is not tamei, as seen from the Kohen Gadol's immersions on Yom Kippur and immersion before Shabbos.
Many customs beyond the letter of the law, such as Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, are ways to give Hashem nachas ruach.
