title.en: Facing the Beis Hamikdash in tefillah

summary.en: The Rav brings Shlomo HaMelech's tefillah that exiled Jews should turn toward the Beis Hamikdash, and explains that in Boro Park facing east is not exact, so one should turn halfway to the south. Above all, one should have in mind that he stands in the Beis Hamikdash, and it is accepted as if he were there.

title.en: A person is where his thought is

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a person is where his thought is, and the Satmar Rav's support from the Gemara about a traveler on Erev Shabbos who fixes his place by a tree near the city. Since one who has the Beis Hamikdash in mind is truly there, he should present himself accordingly.

title.en: Ezra's takanah and doing Hashem's will

summary.en: The Rav tells of Ezra's takanah that one who is tamei from keri must immerse before davening and learning, which was not accepted and was annulled, and notes that some Rishonim keep it for davening. He then recalls his rebbe's teaching, from Mesillas Yesharim, that a devoted servant or child does what the master or parent would like even without being told.

title.en: Bilaam versus Avraham at the Akeidah

summary.en: The Rav brings his rebbe's comparison between Bilaam, who claimed to follow Hashem's word yet tried three times to change His mind, and Avraham Avinu, who went with simcha to the Akeidah without one word of protest though it seemed to undo Hashem's promise. Rashi's reading of their walking together shows that both went with joy.

title.en: Hashem favors taharah

summary.en: The Rav shows that Hashem favors service in purity, from the Kohanim who may not serve when tamei, and concludes that immersion before davening is a midas chassidus. He brings the Rambam's letter that he himself always kept Ezra's takanah though he could not codify a chumrah as halachah, and adds the Kohen Gadol's five immersions, immersion before Shabbos, and the Arizal's immersion on Shabbos morning.

title.en: Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and the mikvah

summary.en: The Rav tells how someone asked Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld whether going to the mikvah was not bittul Torah, and he answered that if a mikvah can make a goy into a Yid, it can make a Yid into a better Yid. The Rav stresses he is not telling anyone to go daily, only that a Yid should want to give Hashem nachas ruach like a child who brings his mother a gift unasked.

title.en: Rabbeinu Tam tefillin, shofar and purity

summary.en: The Rav explains the custom to put on Rabbeinu Tam tefillin after marriage as an extra nachas ruach: both ways of ordering the parshiyos were old practice, the psak followed Rashi, yet the Zohar says both are needed, and after marriage one can be in greater purity. He compares the doubt over shevarim and teruah in shofar, and closes that purity of the body leads to purity of the soul.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that all the mitzvos are counsel for reaching dveikus, attachment to Hashem, and that tefillah, said with the heart, with emunah and facing Yerushalayim, is the clearest form of that attachment.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Zohar that the 613 mitzvos are counsel for reaching dveikus, being attached to Hashem. The soul is already holy; it came down so that the animal-like body should be purified through the mitzvos and share in that attachment. Tefillah is the true dveikus of the heart: the word itself means to attach, like tefillin bound tight, and Dovid HaMelech testifies that Hashem bends His ear to a Jew who prays. The Rav urges davening with the meaning of the words, with a story about a poritz's mistake, and brings Rav Chaim Brisker that one must feel he stands before the King. Even a request for one's needs, a lower, not-for-its-own-sake prayer, fulfills emunah, as two Chassidic stories show. Finally he explains facing Yerushalayim in prayer: a person is where his thoughts are, as the Mishnah on techum Shabbos shows, and he closes with the days of Hod before Shavuos.

en: All 613 mitzvos are counsel for reaching dveikus with Hashem, which has many levels, from total absorption to simply feeling a closeness and a pleasure in it.
The soul is already holy; a person came into the world for the sake of the body, so that through the mitzvos it should be purified and itself attain dveikus.
Tefillah, the service of the heart, is the true dveikus; the word means attaching, as tefillin must be bound tight, and Hashem gives the one who prays His full attention.
One should daven with the meaning of the words and the awareness of standing before the King; one who keeps striving will find his heart opening sooner or later.
Asking Hashem for one's needs, even a small thing, is an act of emunah, the first of the Ten Commandments and the foundation of all mitzvos.
A Jew davens facing Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash, and since a person is where his thoughts are, in his tefillah he is truly there.

title.en: Davening with the heart; the poritz's mistake

summary.en: The Rav speaks of davening with the heart, as in Ahavah Rabbah, brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that such davening would bring Moshiach, says that even mechanical understanding of the words is good, and tells of a poritz whose miscalculation went unnoticed because his mind was not busy, as some Jews' minds are, with accounts during Shemoneh Esrei.

title.en: Before the King; Torah for its own sake

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam and Rav Chaim Brisker that tefillah requires awareness of standing before the King, promises that persistent effort will open the heart, calls emunah the foundation of all mitzvos, and then lays out the levels of learning Torah for its own sake, adding that young bachurim must learn even not for its own sake.

title.en: Praying for needs is emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that praying for livelihood, children or health is tefillah not for its own sake, yet, as the Maharal and Rabbeinu Yonah say, it is a great thing, because it rests on the belief that Hashem can fulfill one's request, which is emunah, the first of the Ten Commandments.

title.en: Two tzaddikim ask for small things

summary.en: The Rav tells how Rabbi Dovid of Tolna delayed entering for the shofar blowing on Rosh Hashanah, ashamed to ask the great King for a roll, until he realized there is no one else to ask, and how a Chernobyler tzaddik asked Hashem that a household helper should not leave, explaining that one must ask Hashem for every small thing.

title.en: Facing Yerushalayim: where one's thought is

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara and Shlomo HaMelech's prayer that one davens toward Eretz Yisrael, Yerushalayim and the Holy of Holies, explains why the Rishonim faced east and the Ba'al HaTanya's siddur southeast, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is, proven from the Mishnah of one who sets his eyes on a tree for his Shabbos boundary.

title.en: In Yerushalayim at prayer; days of Hod

summary.en: The Rav concludes that a Jew davening with kavanah toward Yerushalayim is there in his tefillah, then speaks of Pesach Sheni and the week of Hod leading to Lag BaOmer and Shavuos, bringing the Sfas Emes that the two loaves of Shavuos are Torah and tefillah, and closes with a blessing.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Jewish emunah rests on the national revelation at Sinai and its unbroken tradition, and that our generation, the 'heel' of the body of Klal Yisroel, has emunah without feeling, yet its small avodah is especially precious to Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam and the Kuzari: Jewish faith rests on the whole people standing at Sinai, something no other religion claims, and so the Torah will never be exchanged. Emunah, he says, is not grasped with the intellect, just as a picture is not heard and music is not seen. He then reads the Yismach Moshe's answer to a man troubled by doubts: a tradition received from six hundred thousand eyewitnesses cannot be a lie, since no parent could tell his child about an event nobody saw. Next comes the Bnei Yissaschar's question how the Rambam could write the Moreh Nevuchim if philosophical inquiry is forbidden, answered with the story of the Yismach Moshe and the Rambam's yiras shamayim. Finally the Rav describes every generation, and all of history, as one body of Adam haRishon; ours is the heel, without feeling, yet our small avodah is precious, like the parrot in the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable.

en: Jewish emunah rests on the revelation at Sinai witnessed by the entire nation, which no other religion claims and which cannot be denied.
Hashem cannot be grasped with the intellect; another faculty is needed, just as the eye cannot hear music and the ear cannot see a picture.
Following the Yismach Moshe, a tradition from six hundred thousand eyewitnesses passed from parent to child cannot be a fabrication.
Every generation, and all of Jewish history together, forms one body of Adam haRishon, and each person has the choice to serve Hashem in the way of his place in it.
Ours is the generation of the heel, whose emunah is present but not felt, and therefore its small acts of avodah are especially precious to Hashem.

title.en: Emunah built on Sinai, not on the intellect

summary.en: Recalling the Rambam and the Kuzari, the Rav explains that Jewish faith rests on a revelation the whole nation witnessed, unlike other religions, and cites the Rambam's principle that the Torah will never be exchanged. He lists ways to emunah and argues, with the parable of a picture and a symphony, that Hashem is not grasped by the intellect.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's answer to doubts

summary.en: The Rav reads the Yismach Moshe's reply to a man plagued by doubts in emunah: the proof is not philosophy but the tradition received from six hundred thousand who saw, which no one could have invented and handed to his children. He adds that even other nations accept the miracles of Egypt, and lists the public miracles of the desert and of Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The Bnei Yissaschar's question on the Moreh Nevuchim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar's question: philosophical inquiry weighs both sides, so for a moment one entertains denial; how then could the Rambam write the Moreh Nevuchim? He answers that the Rambam was holy, and tells how the Yismach Moshe asked in Heaven for the Rambam's yiras shamayim and could not bear it.

title.en: The Rambam's katnus and answer before question

summary.en: The Rav relates the Ba'al Shem Tov's comment that what the Yismach Moshe received was only the Rambam's mochin dekatnus, explains gadlus and katnus in tefillah, and concludes that the Rambam felt Hashem even while writing questions, writing for those who had strayed. From the order of Ein Kelokeinu he shows that a Jew must begin with the answer of emunah before asking.

title.en: Each generation as the body of Adam haRishon

summary.en: Bringing the Tanya and a Midrash, the Rav explains that all souls hung from Adam haRishon, from head to toenails, so that each generation is a complete Adam haRishon: the head are the great Torah scholars, the heart the masters of tefillah, the hands the givers of tzedakah. Each person has the choice to use his gift for Hashem or for worldly things, illustrated with Reb Elchonon Wasserman and a wealthy man who gave to colleges.

title.en: Our generation is the heel without feeling

summary.en: The Rav extends the image to all generations: the generation of the desert with Moshe Rabbeinu is the head, the generation of David and Shlomo the throat, and the last generation, ikvesa demeshicha, the heel. The heel has no feeling and stays dark even in the summer sun; so emunah today is present but unfelt, like a tooth pulled after a dentist's injection, unlike the Elul and tefillah of earlier generations.

title.en: The precious avodah of a low generation

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Reb Avraham of Ciechanow's joy at putting on tefillin with our small satisfaction, yet says our avodah is more precious in Heaven than that of earlier generations: holding back from interrupting learning or from idle talk is mesiras nefesh for us. He closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king who delights more in a talking parrot than in his wise ministers.

oneLiner.en: Opening the first chapter of Tanya for bachurim, the Rav explains that every Jew has two souls, a holy one and one from kelipah, and that the lifelong war between them is the very purpose of coming into the world.

abstract.en: The Rav introduces the Tanya's teaching, brought from the Arizal, that every Jew has two souls: one from holiness and one from kelipah, a word meaning a shell, like the shell of a nut. Foreign thoughts in davening do not mean something is wrong with a person; they come from the second soul, and the war against it is why souls that sang with the angels were sent down. Only rare tzaddikim finish the war. He then describes the four kelipos opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name through a rose among thorns and the walnut with its four shells, linking it to 'el ginas egoz yaradti' and to Yechezkel's vision, where the fourth, nogah, is light that passes through a barrier like a window shade. A Jew's body and yetzer come from nogah and can be elevated, chiefly by eating l'shem shamayim. Finally he reads the Tanya's text: Rabbi Chaim Vital's two souls, the sitra achra as the other side of a walled field, the animal soul in the blood, and the four elements.

en: Every Jew has two souls, one from holiness and one from kelipah, a shell that covers the edible fruit.
Foreign thoughts during davening come from the second soul and are no sign that something is wrong with the person.
Almost everyone is sent into the world to wage this war all his life; only rare tzaddikim finish it.
There are four kelipos opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name, like the four shells around the walnut's four sections.
The fourth kelipah, nogah, can be elevated; a Jew's body and yetzer come from it, while the three impure kelipos cannot be.
The animal soul resides in the blood, and from it come all bad traits, built of the four elements opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name.

title.en: Two souls and thoughts in davening

summary.en: The Rav begins the Tanya: every Jew has a soul from holiness and a soul from kelipah, explained through the shell of a nut. He then explains that stray thoughts during davening come from the second soul and do not mean something is wrong with the person.

title.en: Sent down for a lifelong war

summary.en: The Rav explains that only rare tzaddikim finish the war with the yetzer hara, while almost everyone is sent down to wage it all his life. Souls that sang with the angels before the Throne were sent into the world for this war.

title.en: The rose, the walnut and four kelipos

summary.en: The Rav explains the four kelipos opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name with a rose among thorns and the walnut, which grows inside a green bitter shell, a hard shell and a soft skin, with four sections inside. He connects this to the passuk 'el ginas egoz yaradti': the Jewish soul is the garden of nuts.

title.en: Yechezkel's vision and kelipas nogah

summary.en: The Rav brings the first chapter of Yechezkel, read as the haftarah of Shavuos: before seeing the Merkavah the navi passed four barriers, a storm wind, a great cloud, a flashing fire and nogah. He explains nogah as light that comes through a barrier, like sunlight through a window shade, and identifies it with the walnut's fourth skin, which is eaten with the nut.

title.en: Elevating nogah through eating

summary.en: The Rav explains that a gentile's soul and yetzer come from the three impure kelipos, while a Jew's body and yetzer come from nogah, which can be elevated. He shows how an honest Jew eats: netilas yadayim, hamotzi, salt, eating in moderation and with thanks to Hashem, so that he has strength to daven and learn; eaten carelessly, nogah becomes impure.

title.en: The Tanya's text: Rabbi Chaim Vital and the sitra achra

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's opening citation of Rabbi Chaim Vital, the Arizal's disciple, that every Jew has two souls, with the passuk 'u'neshamos ani asisi'. He explains 'sitra achra' as 'the other side' through a field divided by a wall, with fruit and good things on the right and snakes and hornets on the left.

title.en: The animal soul in the blood and the four elements

summary.en: The Rav explains that the second soul resides in the blood, and from it come all bad traits, from four elements of the sitra achra opposite the four holy letters of Hashem's Name. He describes the four elements, fire, air, water and earth, as energy, gas, liquid and solid, and ends that this will be explained further.

catalogTitle: Our Steadfast Faith in Hashem's Salvation ('פירוש על פרק כ “יענך ה' ביום צרה”)

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim chapter 20, Lamenatzeach … Ya'ancha Hashem b'yom tzarah, the Rav explains that in a time of danger before Moshiach a Jew sings and thanks Hashem even before the salvation, because he is certain it will come.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by explaining why he will speak in English, then begins a series on the chapters of Tehillim said in davening, starting with chapter 20 because Klal Yisrael is in an eis tzarah. He recalls how Hashem saved the Jews when Rommel stood at the gates of Eretz Yisrael and in the Six Day War, and brings the Zohar that Yaakov Avinu saved three of his four brachos for the troubles before Moshiach. The troubles before Moshiach are birth pangs; Chazal say a woman in labor sighs seventy times, and the chapter's seventy words match them, its last word, kareinu, being our time. Dovid sings to the One who grants victory and thanks Him before the yeshua. Through the verses he explains Elokei Yaakov, the minchah of a poor man, the request that Hashem's Name be whole, the lessons of history, and that Jews rise after they fall.

en: The Rav says Klal Yisrael is in an eis tzarah and needs great mercy, so he begins with the chapter of Tehillim that is the tefillah for a time of trouble.
The troubles before Moshiach are birth pangs, and the seventy words of the chapter correspond to the seventy sighs of a woman in labor; we are now at its last word, kareinu.
Dovid does not cry in his trouble but sings to the One who grants victory, and thanks Hashem already before the salvation, because he is sure it will come.

Hashem is called the G-d of Yaakov because Yaakov's life was a continuous chain of troubles which he bore with bitachon, and his journeys represent the Jewish people's journey through galus to the geulah.
Hashem does not expect from this generation the avodah of earlier tzaddikim; He regards our small offering like a rich korban.
From history and their own experience Jews know that at moments of seeming despair Hashem helps, and unlike nations who trust in chariots and horses, they rise again after they fall.

Yaakov Avinu as the model of galus

title.en: Why the shiur is in English

summary.en: The Rav asks whether everyone understands Yiddish and decides to speak in English. He explains that Yiddish served as a bond for Jews wandering from land to land in galus, but today it is spoken only in a few communities and most Torah is learned in other languages.

title.en: Tehillim for an eis tzarah; Rommel at the gates

summary.en: The Rav announces that he will learn the chapters of Tehillim said in davening, starting with one suited to the present eis tzarah. He recalls how the Nazi general Rommel reached Alexandria and boasted he would be in Tel Aviv the next morning, how tzaddikim went up to daven, and how that very night the German downfall began.

title.en: Today's danger and Yaakov's reserved brachos

summary.en: The Rav describes the miracles of the Six Day War, when the newspapers predicted the end of the Jewish nation, and says the present quiet is the calm before the storm. He brings the Zohar that Yaakov Avinu used only his weakest bracha for himself and saved the other three for the time before Moshiach, when all nations surround Klal Yisrael, and says we must daven for ourselves and the whole world.

title.en: Birth pangs and the seventy words

summary.en: The Rav explains that the troubles before Moshiach are called chevlei Moshiach, like birth pangs. Chazal say a woman in labor sighs seventy times, and Lamenatzeach has seventy words, which is why it is said for a woman giving birth; Klal Yisrael has now reached the last word, kareinu, and must cry out to Hashem.

title.en: Singing to the One who grants victory

summary.en: The Rav says he draws on several meforshim, among them Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch. He explains that Dovid opens a chapter of trouble with song: when a person has no more eitzos, Hashem must send the yeshua, and lamenatzeach means both the conductor of a choir and the One who grants victory, so Dovid thanks Hashem already before the salvation.

title.en: Ya'ancha Hashem and the G-d of Yaakov

summary.en: On Ya'ancha Hashem b'yom tzarah, yesagevcha shem Elokei Yaakov, the Rav explains with the Ramban that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children. Yaakov's life was all troubles, with Esav, Lavan, Dinah and Yosef, yet he always had bitachon, and his journeys represent Klal Yisrael in galus until the geulah.

title.en: Help from Tziyon and the poor man's minchah

summary.en: The Rav explains, with Rashi, that all tefillos go up through Yerushalayim and the yeshua comes from there. On yizkor kol minchosecha he brings Rashi that a minchah is the poor man's offering, and says Hashem does not expect the avodah of earlier generations but counts our small offering like a fat korban, and Jews sing with joy even amid their troubles.

title.en: Asking that Hashem's Name be whole

summary.en: The Rav brings that tzaddikim in their troubles think only that Hashem's Name is not complete, and ask that it become whole and His kingship be revealed. On atah yadati he says Jews know from history, from the war against Hitler, the Six Day War and the Yom Kippur War, that Hashem helps when all seems lost.

title.en: Chariots and horses; we rise again

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the nations, who worship their own strength, their chariots and today their tanks, with Jews who mention Hashem's Name and draw down chassadim. Nations that fall stay fallen, but Jews rise because they are eternal; he closes that we are in the labor pains, at kareinu, and Hashem will send Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Rav tells from a sefer by the Belzer Rav's gabbai how the Belzer Rav had people speak of a tzaddik so that his merit would save the Jews in a war, and says that today one should speak of the Belzer Rav for the same reason.

abstract.en: The Rav mentions a sefer that came out from the Belzer Rav's gabbai. It tells that during a war in Eretz Yisrael the Belzer Rav sent word to the people in the beis medrash to speak about Reb Shlomke of Zvhil, who had already passed away, so that his merit would stand by the Jews against their enemies; a quarter of an hour later the gabbai came out to ask whether they were indeed speaking about him. The Rav then describes a Friday night of that war when the Belzer Rav stood by the candles for hours, repeating the words 'hapores sukkas shalom', and the Jews saw miracles beyond nature: the Arabs, who could have taken the land from an unprepared population, fled. He concludes that today one should speak of the Belzer Rav so that his merit brings a great yeshuah, and adds a word about safety: wherever a person is, only Hashem can help.

en: According to the gabbai's sefer, the Belzer Rav had the people speak about Reb Shlomke of Zvhil during a war, so that the tzaddik's merit would help the Jews against their enemies.
The Rav stresses that the victory in that war could not be measured in natural terms: few Jews, unprepared, against a vast Arab population that simply fled.
On a Friday night of that war the Belzer Rav stood by the candles for hours, repeating 'hapores sukkas shalom', and the Jews saw miracles beyond nature.
The Rav says that today one should speak about the Belzer Rav, so that his merit brings the Jews a great yeshuah.
Asked whether it is safe to travel around there, the Rav answers that nobody knows it is safer elsewhere, since wherever one is Hashem must help.

title.en: The Belzer Rav and the merit of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav tells from the gabbai's sefer how the Belzer Rav had people speak of Reb Shlomke of Zvhil during a war, and how he stood by the Shabbos candles while the Jews saw miracles. He says today one should speak of the Belzer Rav for a yeshuah, and answers a question about safety: wherever one is, Hashem must help.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the seven weeks of Sefirah are given to refine each of the middos so that they serve Hashem in holiness, since good middos come before the Torah, and he describes the final preparations for Shavuos: the night of learning and the mikveh at dawn.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that Shavuos needs the longest preparation of any Yom Tov: seven weeks in which each middah is purified, since every middah can be holy or the reverse. Chesed is love, as when the Jews followed Hashem into the desert without calculations; the Ba'al Shem Tov shows from the passuk that forbidden love is chesed gone astray. Gevurah means fearing Hashem and no person; tiferes means beauty for Hashem, not competing over shtreimels and houses. Netzach and hod are the two legs that let a person stand: winning for the truth and conceding to it. Since derech eretz comes before the Torah, a ben Torah must be refined, which is why Rebbes abolished pushing and grabbing at the tish. The weekly chapters of Pirkei Avos match the weeks of Sefirah. He then describes Rosh Chodesh Sivan, the three days of hagbalah, learning on Shavuos night to become a full vessel, and the special holiness of the Shavuos mikveh.

en: The seven weeks before Shavuos are for refining the seven middos, because each middah can be in holiness or, chas veshalom, the reverse.
Chesed means love: serving Hashem with a love so strong that one makes no calculations, as the Jews followed Him into the desert.
Gevurah in holiness is fear of Hashem alone, and tiferes in holiness is beauty dedicated to Hashem and His mitzvos, not to outdoing others.
Netzach and hod are the two legs that let a person stand: prevailing for the truth and conceding to it, each of which can be holy or impure.
Derech eretz comes before the Torah, so a ben Torah must have refined middos and must not push or act wildly, even in the name of Chassidus.
Pirkei Avos is learned in the weeks before Shavuos because it teaches middos, and each week's chapter matches that week's sefirah.
The night of Shavuos is spent learning so that one becomes a full vessel able to receive the Torah, and the mikveh at dawn on Shavuos carries a holiness found at no other time of the year.

title.en: Seven weeks to refine the middos; chesed

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shavuos is prepared for over seven weeks of refining the middos, and that chesed is love: the love with which the Jews followed Hashem into the desert. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of the passuk that calls a forbidden union 'chesed' to show that chesed can be misdirected, and says the first week of Sefirah is for purifying it.

title.en: Gevurah and tiferes in holiness

summary.en: Gevurah is fear: of Hashem, never of people, as the Torah tells a dayan not to fear any man, and as the Yiddish prayer 'Got fun Avrohom' asks. Tiferes is beauty: beautiful tefillin, a sefer Torah or a fine old sefer is holy, while competing over houses, cars and ever taller shtreimels is its impure opposite.

title.en: Right over left; netzach and hod as two legs

summary.en: Each middah corresponds to a limb: chesed and gevurah are the right and left hands, which is why the right side is given precedence, as in putting on the right sleeve first. Netzach and hod are the legs that let a person stand: prevailing and conceding, both of which must be for the truth and not for showing off. He touches on the week of malchus, when Tachanun is not said.

title.en: Derech eretz before Torah: no pushing at the tish

summary.en: Because derech eretz comes before the Torah, a ben Torah must work on good middos and must not push or act wildly in the name of Chassidus. The Rav tells how the previous Gerrer Rebbe abolished pushing to the Rebbe, how at the Stoliner Rebbe's tish the kugel is passed around without pushing, and how grabbing shirayim, once an expression of holy love, has become bad middos.

title.en: Pirkei Avos, Rosh Chodesh Sivan and Shavuos night

summary.en: The Rav shows how each week's chapter of Pirkei Avos matches that week's sefirah, since Pirkei Avos teaches middos. He then describes the added preparation from Rosh Chodesh Sivan, when the Avodas Yisrael says to learn each day's pesukim, the three days of hagbalah, and learning all night on Shavuos, because in Torah a full vessel receives more.

title.en: The Shavuos mikveh and davening with strength

summary.en: The Rav explains that a kosher mikveh purifies and sanctifies through holy names, that some mikvaos are holier than others, and that the mikveh at dawn on Shavuos has a holiness of its own; he tells of the salty spring water found when the Satmar Rav built his mikveh. He closes by saying one should rest before davening on Shavuos morning so as to daven with mind and heart.

oneLiner.en: Learning the opening of Tanya with bachurim, the Rav explains the two souls in every Jew, the animal soul that dwells in the blood, and how the four elements give rise to the bad middos: anger and pride, lust for pleasure, frivolity and jokes, and sadness and laziness.

abstract.en: The Rav reads that, according to R' Chaim Vital, every Jew has two souls, the yetzer tov from holiness and the yetzer hara from the kelipah, and the person himself must choose which to listen to, since, as Eliyahu told the people, one cannot stand on two sides. The soul of the kelipah dwells in the blood, as the passuk says that the soul of flesh is in the blood; it is the animal soul, which seeks only its desires, and this is why eating blood is forbidden. He explains the four kelipos of Yechezkel's vision and kelipas nogah. A long digression links colors to the sefiros: red is blood and gevurah, white is chesed, green is life, which is why red means stop. He then shows the four elements behind the bad middos: fire brings anger and pride, water brings pleasures, wind brings frivolity and jokes, with stories of the Ropshitzer and the Belzer Rav, and earth brings sadness and laziness.

en: Every person has two souls, the yetzer tov from holiness and the yetzer hara from the kelipah, and the person must choose which one to listen to.
The animal soul dwells in the blood and seeks only its desires; therefore the Torah forbade eating blood, which would strengthen it.
Each color reflects one of the ten sayings and sefiros: red is gevurah and blood, white is chesed, green is life.
Everything in the world is made of the four elements, fire, wind, water and earth, and the bad middos come from them.
Anger and pride both come from fire, which always rises; anger comes from a person's sense that everything must go as he wants.
Frivolity, jokes and idle talk come from wind: one leaves them with nothing, while sadness and laziness come from earth, which sinks down.

title.en: Two souls in every person

summary.en: The Rav reads from R' Chaim Vital that every Jew, tzaddik or rasha, has two souls, the yetzer tov from holiness and the yetzer hara from the kelipah, and a third, the person himself, must choose between them. He brings Eliyahu's words that one cannot stand on two sides.

title.en: The animal soul in the blood

summary.en: The Rav explains that the soul of the kelipah is clothed in the blood and is the animal soul, which wants only food, drink and desires. He describes the four kelipos and kelipas nogah, and explains why eating blood is forbidden and why the lifeblood leaves at shechitah.

title.en: Colors, sefiros and the traffic light

summary.en: The Rav explains that the nations kept things from Noach without knowing why: red means stop because red is blood and gevurah, green means go because green is life, and white is chesed. This is why doctors, bakers and those wearing a kittel on Yom Kippur dress in white.

title.en: The four elements and the fire of anger

summary.en: Returning to the text, the Rav explains the four elements and compares them to solid, liquid, gas and energy, shows how a burning table releases fire, wind and water while earth remains, and links them to the four letters of Hashem's name. Anger comes from the element of fire, which is why an angry man turns red, like the rising and setting sun.

title.en: Pride rises like fire; pleasure from water

summary.en: The Rav explains that anger and pride are one thing: a man gets angry because things did not go as he wants, while a humble man never gets angry; both come from fire, which always rises. The desire for pleasures comes from water, and this is why people drink tasteless water with relish.

title.en: Wind: frivolity, jokes and the Ropshitzer

summary.en: The Rav explains that frivolity, jokes and idle talk come from wind: they hold nothing, and after a wedding full of a badchan's jokes one leaves with nothing and no more yiras Shamayim. He contrasts the jests of great tzaddikim, telling how the Linsker Rav listened to his son the Ropshitzer's wedding rhymes and found Kabbalah in every word.

title.en: Tzaddikim's speech; sadness and laziness from earth

summary.en: The Rav tells how R' Aharon of Belz heard holy matters in his father's talk about politics, showing that a tzaddik's simple words hold yichudim. He then explains that sadness and laziness come from earth, which sinks down, and describes people who greet a new day without joy or desire, and closes that good natural middos also come from the four elements.

catalogTitle: Thanking Hashem - An Endless Endeavor (מזמור לתודה)

oneLiner.en: Starting from Mizmor l'Sodah, the Rav shows that thanking Hashem is an endless task: every breath, every hidden miracle and every rescue calls for thanks, and Hashem even arranged the miracle at the Yam Suf so that Jews could come back and thank Him there.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Mizmor l'Sodah and calls the chance to thank Hashem one of His greatest gifts. That is why each person says Modim d'Rabbanan himself, and why it ends with thanks for being able to thank. David HaMelech closes Tehillim with praise for every breath, and Nishmas admits that we could not thank even for one of His countless favors; the body alone is a daily miracle. The four who must thank in Tehillim 107 are only samples, and the Gemara requires ten people, two of them Rabbanan, for Birkas HaGomel: a wise man is needed to explain the kindness, and a second one shows there is always more to say. The short eating time of the korban todah increases pirsumei nisa, which leads to Chanukah, women's obligation in it, and gratitude as the root of avodas Hashem. He ends with the Chasam Sofer on why the Egyptians drowned in the Yam Suf and not the Nile.

en: The Rav says the opportunity to thank Hashem, and the realization that it is a privilege, is itself one of Hashem's greatest gifts.
Thanks can never be finished: Tehillim ends with praise for every breath, and Nishmas says one cannot thank even for a single favor among thousands.
The four kinds of people who must thank are only samples, reminders that one must thank Hashem for everything.
Recognizing Hashem's hidden kindnesses takes a chacham who works on hakaras hatov, which is why Birkas HaGomel needs two Rabbanan.
Mitzvos of pirsumei nisa, publicizing a miracle, outweigh other mitzvos, and even women are obligated in them.
Gratitude is the greatest obligation in avodas Hashem: the more a person appreciates, the more of a tzaddik he becomes.
Hashem drowned the Egyptians in the Yam Suf and not in the Nile so that Jews could come to the place of the miracle and make a bracha.

title.en: Mizmor l'Sodah and Modim d'Rabbanan

summary.en: After a brief exchange before the shiur, the Rav opens with Mizmor l'Sodah and calls the chance to thank Hashem one of His greatest gifts. He explains why each person says Modim d'Rabbanan himself, and that it ends with thanks for being able to thank.

title.en: For every breath: Tehillim and Nishmas

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tehillim is mostly hoda'ah, and that David HaMelech ends it feeling he must thank for every breath. He brings Nishmas, that one cannot thank even for one favor, and describes the human body as a daily miracle.

title.en: The four who must thank are only samples

summary.en: The Rav brings the kapitel of Tehillim with the four who are rescued and must thank, and explains that they are only samples for thanking for everything. He brings the Gemara that Birkas HaGomel is said before ten with two Rabbanan, and says people notice their teeth only when they ache.

title.en: Why two Rabbanan at Birkas HaGomel

summary.en: The Rav explains that only a chacham who works on hakaras hatov sees Hashem's kindness in everything, even in what seems bad. Two are needed so that the second shows there is more to say after the first finished: thanking Hashem never ends.

title.en: The korban todah and pirsumei nisa

summary.en: The Rav explains that the korban todah, unlike other shelamim, may be eaten only for a day and a night until chatzos, and brings the mefarshim that this makes the owner invite more people and publicize Hashem's kindness. He concludes that mitzvos of pirsumei nisa outweigh other mitzvos.

title.en: Chanukah, hidden miracles and gratitude

summary.en: With Chanukah approaching, the Rav explains that owing thanks makes a person subordinate to his benefactor, that only Hashem knows the miracles He does daily, and that gratitude is the greatest obligation in avodas Hashem. He explains why women are obligated in Chanukah lights and the four cups, and begins the case of choosing between Kiddush wine and Chanukah lights.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: why the Yam Suf and not the Nile

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's question why the prohibition of returning to Mitzrayim is mentioned at the Yam Suf, and why the Egyptians were not drowned in the Nile, measure for measure. The answer: one makes a bracha at the place of a miracle, and since Jews may not return to Mitzrayim, Hashem made the miracle where they could come and thank Him.

oneLiner.en: The Rav sees in the fall of the rulers of Yishmael and other events of the time signs of the approach of Moshiach, and calls for strengthening in Torah, tefillah and chesed as the new zman begins.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls that when Mubarak of Egypt fell he had spoken of a Midrash brought by the Ba'al HaTurim: the twelve princes of Yishmael are listed just before 'these are the generations of Yitzchak', and when those princes fall it is a sign that Moshiach, who comes from Yitzchak, will come. Since then the rulers have fallen one after another. He adds, as a tradition of tzaddikim, that when a great ruler falls among the nations, his heavenly prince has fallen first. We live in a great time and should be shaken by it; to be saved from the birth pangs of Moshiach he brings the Gemara and speaks of Torah, tefillah and chesed. After mentioning an earthquake in America, he speaks of every Jew as a shaliach of Hashem, of the historic nature of the time, and closes with a thought from the haftarah: water, which is Torah, flows to the low place.

en: The Ba'al HaTurim brings a Midrash that the fall of the princes of Yishmael is a sign that Moshiach, from Yitzchak, will come.
The Rav points out that the rulers of Yishmael have fallen one after another, and says there is no doubt about it.
When a great ruler of the nations falls, it is a sign that his heavenly prince has fallen first.
To be saved from the birth pangs of Moshiach, the Rav speaks of strengthening in Torah, tefillah and chesed.
Every Jew is a shaliach of the Ribono shel Olam to spread Torah and yiras Shamayim, and must take the present historic time seriously.
Water, which the Gemara says is Torah, flows from a high place to a low one; the Torah stays with one who makes himself low.

title.en: The fall of the princes of Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav recalls the Ba'al HaTurim's Midrash that the fall of the princes of Yishmael signals the coming of Moshiach, notes how the rulers have fallen one after another, and explains that their heavenly princes fall first. He calls for strengthening in Torah, tefillah and chesed to be saved from the birth pangs of Moshiach.

title.en: A historic time and our shlichus

summary.en: The Rav mentions an earthquake felt in America, says every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem to spread Torah and yiras Shamayim, and urges taking this historic time seriously. He closes with the haftarah's call to the water, which is Torah and flows to the low place, and a blessing for the new zman.

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches bachurim that good middos are the precondition for Torah, that a person's middos reach even into his property and his friends, and that from bnei Torah, like a silk shirt, far more is demanded than the letter of the law.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rabbi Chaim Vital's question in Shaarei Kedushah: why does the Torah hardly speak of middos? The answer is that derech eretz precedes Torah: the Torah was given to people who already have middos. He urges the bachurim going to camp to stress middos and be role models. Middos are hidden in the laws of damages: a person's property is an extension of his nefesh, as the story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey shows, so an honest owner's ox does not damage, and a tzaddik's belongings and even friends absorb his soul. Through Rabbah bar bar Chana's porters and the Zohar's stringency on netilas yadayim, he explains that the Torah has levels matching levels of the soul, and more is demanded of a ben Torah. A spot ruins a silk shirt but not a potato sack. He closes with Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin, who refused to sign the cherem and merited a chain of generations.

en: The Torah hardly speaks of middos explicitly because derech eretz precedes Torah: middos are a precondition for receiving it.
The laws of damages carry a lesson in middos: a person's property is part of his nefesh, so the way his animal behaves reflects his own middos.
The Torah has levels, pshat, remez, drush and sod, matching the levels of the soul, and the higher a person stands the more is demanded of him.
Bnei Torah are like a silk shirt: a small flaw in middos that would not matter elsewhere ruins them and causes a chillul Hashem.
For bnei Torah, going beyond the letter of the law is itself the law.

title.en: Why the Torah is silent about middos

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbi Chaim Vital's question why the Torah hardly speaks of middos, and answers that derech eretz precedes Torah: middos are a precondition. He then tells the bachurim going to camp to stress middos and be role models for others.

title.en: Damages and the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair

summary.en: The Rav shows that the laws of damages in Bava Kamma teach respect for another's property, and explains the Mishnah's 'I made its damage possible' to mean that a person's property is part of his nefesh. He proves it from the Gemara's story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey, which would not eat untithed grain.

title.en: An honest owner's ox does not damage

summary.en: The Rav explains that an honest Jew's ox will not damage, and reads the kinds of damage (goring, eating, trampling) as reflections of the owner's own middos. From the same idea he explains why a tzaddik's belongings are precious and why a baal middos makes his friends into baalei middos.

title.en: Rabbah bar bar Chana and the porters

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara's story of Rabbah bar bar Chana, whose porters broke his wine barrels: Rav ruled that he must forgo the damage and even pay their wages, citing 'that you may walk in the way of the good'. He then raises a parallel question: why does the Zohar forbid walking four amos before washing in the morning when the Shulchan Aruch does not?

title.en: Levels of Torah, levels of the soul

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah has four levels, pshat, remez, drush and sod, matching the levels of the soul, nefesh, ruach and neshamah, and brings the Arizal on receiving the extra souls of Shabbos. A simple Jew fulfils the pshat; a ben Torah must do more, and a higher Jew must keep the sod of the Zohar. This is what Rav told Rabbah bar bar Chana.

title.en: The potato sack and the silk shirt

summary.en: The Rav gives a parable: a paint spot on a potato sack does not matter, but a small spot ruins a silk shirt for a wedding. Bnei Torah are silk; poor middos in them, like not greeting people or not standing up for an elderly man on the bus, are a chillul Hashem. For them, going beyond the letter of the law is the law.

title.en: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin and the cherem

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Vilna Gaon, fearing another false messiah like Shabbsai Tzvi, opposed the Ba'al Shem Tov and had his students sign a cherem against the chassidim, and only Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin refused. He explained this from the Akeidah: Hashem Himself commanded Avraham to slaughter Yitzchak, but an angel was enough to stop him, so a command to harm a Jew is not accepted even from a great angel.

title.en: A chain of generations as the reward

summary.en: The Rav lists chassidic dynasties where son after son were great tzaddikim, and notes that among the Litvish this is not found, except for the descendants of Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin, the Brisker family. He brings that this was his reward for refusing to harm a Jew, and closes that one must work on middos between man and his fellow even more than on other halachos.

oneLiner.en: The Rav traces how the secrets of the Torah were revealed in three stages, from Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai through the Arizal to the Ba'al Shem Tov, tells of Rabbi Chaim Vital and the spring of Gichon, and begins Tanya's teaching that every Jew has two souls, the animal soul residing in the blood.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the three stages in which the secrets of the Torah came down. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai revealed them first, in the Zohar and Tikkunei Zohar, yet afterwards they remained with single individuals in each generation, such as the Ramban and Rashba. Then Heaven revealed to the Arizal that the preparation for Moshiach had begun, and Rabbi Chaim Vital wrote his teachings down in Etz Chaim and Pri Etz Chaim. The third stage is the Ba'al Shem Tov, who taught how to use these secrets in serving Hashem; the Toldos, the Tanya and the Me'or Einayim lay the foundations of Chassidus. The Rav then tells how Rabbi Chaim Vital was asked to reopen the spring of Gichon that Chizkiyahu had stopped, and what the Arizal told him. Finally he begins Tanya chapter one: a Jew has two souls, and the animal soul lives in the blood, which is why the Torah forbids eating blood.

en: The secrets of the Torah came down in three stages: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the Arizal, and the Ba'al Shem Tov.
Even after the Zohar, the secrets of the Torah were passed down only to single individuals in each generation, such as the Ramban and the Rashba.
The Arizal was told from Heaven that the preparation for the days of Moshiach had begun and that the secrets should now be spread.
The Ba'al Shem Tov taught how to use the secrets of the Torah in serving Hashem, in davening, learning, and even in the street and in business.
Following Tanya, the Rav teaches that every Jew has two souls, while a non-Jew has only one, the evil inclination.
The animal soul, the force of life, is a spiritual power that lies in the blood, which is why the Torah forbids eating blood.

title.en: From Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai to the Arizal

summary.en: The Rav explains that the secrets of the Torah passed through three stages. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai revealed them in the Zohar and Tikkunei Zohar, but they stayed with individuals like the Ramban and Rashba, until the Arizal was told to spread them and Rabbi Chaim Vital wrote them down in Etz Chaim and Pri Etz Chaim.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and the seforim of Chassidus

summary.en: The Rav describes the third stage, the Ba'al Shem Tov, who taught how to use the secrets in serving Hashem, and names the Toldos, the Tanya and the Me'or Einayim as the foundational seforim of Chassidus. He explains that the first chapters of Tanya give knowledge, and later chapters show how to use it in avodah.

title.en: Rabbi Chaim Vital and the spring of Gichon

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Arab ruler of Jerusalem asked Rabbi Chaim Vital to reopen the spring of Gichon that King Chizkiyahu had stopped up. Rabbi Chaim Vital was afraid and left for the Arizal, who told him that had he opened it Moshiach would soon have come, and that it was now too late.

title.en: Two souls, and the life that lies in the blood

summary.en: The Rav begins Tanya chapter one: a Jew has two souls, a non-Jew only one, apart from rare righteous gentiles. He explains that the animal soul is the mysterious force of life that no scientist can explain, a spiritual power lying in the blood, which is why the Torah in this week's parsha forbids eating blood. He ends by arranging the time of next week's shiur.

catalogTitle: Serving Hashem with Joy; A Product of Appreciation (מזמור לתודה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that avodas Hashem rests on gratitude, which is why the morning prayers open with Mizmor Lesodah, and that true service must also be filled with joy.

abstract.en: Continuing Mizmor Lesodah, the Rav teaches that a person who is not grateful to people will not be grateful to Hashem; ingratitude is animal-like, as shown by a bar mitzvah boy who complained about a hand-me-down suit. Gratitude lets a person see what Hashem does for him every moment, which is why Modim, Modeh Ani and Mizmor Lesodah come first, and on Shabbos we thank Hashem even for His hidden conduct of history. Adam HaRishon's first words to Hashem were ungrateful, while Bikurim, the first gift, declares that a Jew is not ungrateful. The Rav reads from the will of a tzaddik who thanked Hashem for every small thing: a private room, a sharpened knife, glasses that did not break. Thanksgiving remains even in the future. Finally, Mizmor Lesodah calls for serving Hashem with joy: Ish stands for love, fear and joy, and a clear devar halacha before davening brings that joy.

en: The Rav says avodas Hashem is built on thankfulness, and one who is not grateful to people will not be grateful to Hashem.
The first thing in prayer and in the day is thanks: Modeh Ani on waking, and Mizmor Lesodah right after Baruch She'amar.
One thanks Hashem both for the good one sees and for what one does not yet understand, believing that all is for the good of Klal Yisroel.
Through the will of a tzaddik, the Rav shows how one can thank Hashem for every small and large thing, even something seemingly bad.
Avodas Hashem is incomplete without simcha; a mitzvah needs love, fear and joy.

title.en: A person must be thankful

summary.en: The Rav opens Mizmor Lesodah by teaching that a mensch must be grateful, that ingratitude to people leads to ingratitude to Hashem, and illustrates with a bar mitzvah boy who complained about his hand-me-down suit.

title.en: Thanks comes first in davening

summary.en: The Rav explains Modim and why Mizmor Lesodah opens the psalms after Baruch She'amar; on Shabbos one thanks Hashem for His hidden conduct of history, and the day itself begins with Modeh Ani.

title.en: Adam's ingratitude and the Bikurim

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Adam HaRishon, whose first conversation with Hashem showed ingratitude for his wife, with Bikurim, the first gift, through which a Jew declares he is not ungrateful; he ties this to the hundred daily brachos and the hundredth chapter of Tehillim.

title.en: The will of a tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav introduces a sefer by a tzaddik of about two hundred years ago, praised by the Rebbe of Lublin, explains when a pure person may write about himself, and begins reading how the tzaddik thanked Hashem for both good and bad, and for his private room.

title.en: Thanking for every small thing

summary.en: The Rav continues the tzaddik's will: he thanked Hashem for good news from his children, for what he could buy, for a sharpened knife, a remembered item, glasses that did not break and a found snuffbox; the Rav then explains the two meanings of hodaah and that thanksgiving will remain even in the future.

title.en: Serving Hashem with joy

summary.en: From Mizmor Lesodah the Rav teaches that avodas Hashem must be with simcha: the Levi'im's song supplied joy to a korban, Ish stands for love, fear and joy, and a clear devar halacha before davening brings the joy that tefillah needs.

oneLiner.en: The Rav tells how the Sekulener Rebbe, warned by a Communist commissar never to come again, went once more with mesirus nefesh to plead for an arrested Jew and freed him.

abstract.en: The Rav tells a story of the Sekulener Rebbe in Russia, who was deeply involved in pidyon shevuyim and freed hundreds of Jews through his connections with the Communist authorities. Once, when he came to a commissar to plead for a Jew, the commissar told him that he had always listened to him because he was a true 'communist': one who keeps nothing for himself and gives everything, even his life, for others. But he warned him never to come again to plead for Jews, or he would shoot him. Then a Jew was arrested and faced trial. The Sekulener Rebbe asked the Potiker Rebbe to daven for him, and although he was told he need not risk himself, he answered that for the other Jew it was a matter of life, and he must go. The Potiker Rebbe davened all day; that night the Sekulener Rebbe returned joyful: the commissar had thrown him down the stairs, but freed the Jew.

en: The Sekulener Rebbe was deeply involved in pidyon shevuyim in Russia and freed hundreds of Jews through his connections with the Communists.
The commissar called him a true 'communist', since he kept nothing for himself and gave everything, even his life, for others.
Though threatened with death if he returned, he went again to plead for an arrested Jew, saying that for the other Jew it was a matter of life.
He came back joyful: he had been thrown down the stairs, but the Jew was freed.

title.en: The Sekulener Rebbe and the commissar

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Sekulener Rebbe, who freed many Jews in Russia, was warned by a commissar never to return, yet went again to plead for an arrested Jew while the Potiker Rebbe davened for him, and came back joyful that the Jew was freed.

oneLiner.en: Before the summer break, the Rav tells bachurim that the fallen months of Tamuz and Av are a time to repair what the meraglim spoiled, by going away as Hashem's shluchim and by working on good middos, above all sensitivity to another Jew's feelings.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by explaining that Tamuz and Av are lofty months that fell through the sin of the meraglim, and that the higher a thing is, the deeper it falls. He pairs these months with Reuven and Shimon, who lost their precedence, and shows that the parshiyos of Korach and Pinchas, read as Tamuz and Av begin, tell of the fall of their nesiim; yet whatever falls will be raised again, and these months hold sparks of Moshiach. Since the meraglim failed as shluchim, a bachur leaving home for the summer goes as Hashem's shliach and must remember whose shliach he is; he brings the Chasam Sofer's resolution of who sent the meraglim. Because the churban came from sinas chinam, camp life among friends is the time to work on middos. He then gives many examples of sensitivity to others: Rashi on Yosef's pit, a Gerrer Rebbe's reason why no one says she'asani kohen, not correcting a ba'al korei, knocking before entering, writing clearly, choosing a child's name, and stories of the Berditchever Rav and Rabbi Akiva Eiger.

en: Tamuz and Av are very high months that were damaged by the meraglim, and whatever falls will in the end be raised again.
Going away for the summer is a shlichus from Hashem that repairs the meraglim's journey, and one must remember whose shliach one is.
The Beis HaMikdash was destroyed through bad middos, sinas chinam, so in Tamuz and Av, especially living with friends in camp, one must work on middos, and good middos rebuild Yerushalayim.
Good middos mean thinking of another's feelings and never embarrassing him, even in small matters like a ba'al korei's slip, knocking on a door or writing clearly.
Consideration for another Jew outweighs a hiddur mitzvah and one's own honor, as the stories of the Berditchever Rav and Rabbi Akiva Eiger show.

title.en: Tamuz and Av: high months that fell

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tamuz and Av were meant to be the most joyous months but were damaged by the meraglim, who set out at the end of Sivan and returned on Tisha b'Av. He illustrates with a stone: the higher the place it falls from, the deeper it sinks.

title.en: Reuven, Shimon, Korach and Pinchas

summary.en: The Rav pairs Tamuz and Av with Reuven and Shimon, who lost their precedence among the degalim, and notes that Parshas Korach and Parshas Pinchas, read as these months begin, tell of the fall of their nesiim. Yet what falls will rise: Korach will yet be Kohen Gadol, and Tamuz and Av hold sparks of Moshiach, who according to the Midrash is born on Tisha b'Av.

title.en: The summer as a shlichus from Hashem

summary.en: The Rav says that leaving home for the summer, at the season the meraglim set out, is a shlichus from Hashem that must repair their failure; one may exercise to stay healthy for learning, but must not forget whose shliach one is. He brings the Chasam Sofer, who resolves whether Hashem or the people sent the meraglim: they failed because they went as shluchim of the people.

title.en: Middos among friends rebuild Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav says the main work of camp, where bachurim eat, sleep and live together, is middos: helping a friend and taking care not to hurt him. Since the Beis HaMikdash fell through sinas chinam, as in the story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, these months are the time to fix middos, and good middos build Yerushalayim.

title.en: Yosef's pit and the brachah no kohen says

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Zalman Sorotzkin on Rashi's comment that Yosef's empty pit had snakes and scorpions: the Torah only hints at it, since one may not speak ill even of a pit in Eretz Yisrael. He then brings a Gerrer Rebbe's answer why a kohen does not say a brachah she'asani kohen: it would shame the other Jews, who lost the kehunah through the eigel.

title.en: The camel, the ba'al korei and a knock on the door

summary.en: The Rav brings a Midrash that the Torah first states the camel's sign of purity before its sign of impurity. He cites poskim that one should not correct a ba'al korei's slip that does not change the meaning, so as not to shame him, and teaches that one knocks and waits before entering even one's own home.

title.en: Clear writing and a child's name

summary.en: The Rav says one should write letters, house numbers and the name on a mailbox clearly so others need not strain. He then warns parents not to give a child an old-fashioned name that will make it a target of mockery, with an example of a girl named Yente and a boy in Bnei Brak who was teased for his name.

title.en: The Berditchever Rav, Rabbi Akiva Eiger, and a blessing

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Berditchever Rav warned against putting 'blood' into matzos, meaning pushing exhausted widows to bake faster, and how Rabbi Akiva Eiger hid his learning for the seven days of sheva brachos so as not to outshine another chasan. He closes with a blessing for a successful summer and for Tamuz and Av to turn to joy.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Avraham Avinu took gifts from Pharaoh but refused the king of Sodom, showing that his descent to Mitzrayim was both wrong and right, and that Pharaoh's gifts were a sign for his children's leaving Mitzrayim with great wealth.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a contradiction: Avraham Avinu refused any gift from the king of Sodom, yet he told Sarah to say she was his sister so that Pharaoh would give him gifts. He brings the Ramban, who faults Avraham for leaving Eretz Yisrael in the famine and endangering Sarah, and says this caused the exile in Mitzrayim, and he contrasts it with the Zohar, where an angel assured Avraham. He finds the same clash between the Midrash and the Zohar on Yaakov bowing to Esav. To resolve it he explains the four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, which do not always fit together, and shows from halachic examples, fasting for a dream on Shabbos and the nazir's korban, that one act can be both wrong and right. Avraham's descent caused the galus but the galus purified his children. Following the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, Pharaoh's gifts sealed that Klal Yisrael would leave Mitzrayim with wealth, while a rasha's money carries his tumah.

en: Avraham refused the king of Sodom's gifts but sought Pharaoh's gifts, an apparent contradiction the Rav sets out to resolve.
The Ramban faults Avraham for going down to Mitzrayim without permission and endangering Sarah, and says this brought the galus of Mitzrayim, while the Zohar says an angel assured him.
The four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, usually fit into one another but sometimes contradict, and both sides can be true.
One act can be both a mitzvah and an aveirah, as with fasting for a dream on Shabbos and the nazir who must bring a korban; the question is which outweighs the other.
Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim was wrong, since it brought the galus, and right, since the galus purified his children.
By the Ramban's principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, every stage of Avraham's stay in Mitzrayim foreshadows the exile and redemption of his descendants.
Avraham took Pharaoh's gifts only for his children, to seal that they would leave with wealth, while he refused Sodom's money because a rasha's money carries his tumah.

title.en: Gifts from Pharaoh, none from Sodom

summary.en: The Rav recounts how Avraham rescued Lot and the captives from the four kings and refused anything from the king of Sodom. He contrasts this with Mitzrayim, where Avraham told Sarah to say she was his sister so that he would benefit, and took Pharaoh's gifts.

title.en: The Ramban and the Zohar on going to Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban, who criticizes Avraham for leaving Eretz Yisrael in the famine and endangering Sarah, and says this caused the galus of Mitzrayim. He notes that the Ramban drew on the Zohar, yet the Zohar says an angel assured Avraham, while elsewhere it says he went without permission, leaving many contradictions.

title.en: Yaakov bowing to Esav; the four levels of Torah

summary.en: The Rav shows the same clash between the Midrash, which faults Yaakov for humbling himself before Esav, and the Zohar, which calls it wise because it made Esav grow haughty to his downfall. He then explains pshat, remez, drush and sod, which usually fit into one another but sometimes contradict.

title.en: Both right: examples from halacha

summary.en: The Rav brings examples where pshat and sod point different ways and both are right, depending on a person's madreigah. He shows from fasting for a bad dream on Shabbos, and from the nazir who must bring a korban for depriving himself of wine, that one act can be both right and wrong, and concludes that Yaakov knew both views and chose to bow because the benefit outweighed the harm.

title.en: Avraham was wrong and right

summary.en: The Rav applies this to Avraham: going down to Mitzrayim was wrong, since it brought the galus, yet right, since the servitude of Mitzrayim purified his children and raised them in kedushah. So the Ramban, who says he was wrong and punished, and the Zohar, which says he was right, are both true.

title.en: The deeds of the fathers: a sign for the children

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban's rule that what happened to the Avos is a sign of what will happen to their descendants, and traces the parallels: the famine, Sarah taken by Pharaoh, the plagues that freed her, and Pharaoh's gifts, foreshadowing Klal Yisrael's going down, enslavement, plagues and exodus with wealth. Avraham knew this, so he took the gifts only for his children.

title.en: Sealing the prophecy; the money of a rasha

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Bris bein haBesarim came before the trip to Mitzrayim, and that a prophecy can change but a symbolic act of the Avos cannot, so Avraham took Pharaoh's money to secure the redemption with wealth. He refused Sodom's money because a rasha's money carries his tumah, and answers why the Yidden could take Mitzrayim's wealth: Hashem purified it, as the passuk in Tehillim indicates.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that ours is the generation of the heel, ikvesa d'Meshicha, whose one mitzvah is emunah, so that even in wartime news a Jew must see only Hashem's hand.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that Chavakuk established all the mitzvos on one, 'tzaddik be'emunaso yichyeh', and explains that the last generations must hold on to emunah and hashgacha pratis. With the news from Eretz Yisroel, he says, a Jew should worry for his brothers but never think that a prime minister or general decides the war; Hashem alone does, as the missiles that miss show. He brings a Midrash that the generations are limbs of Adam HaRishon, ours being the heel. He then explains what a dybbuk is and tells how R' Yehoshua of Belz and, in Radin, R' Elchonon Wasserman on behalf of the Chofetz Chaim drove one out. The Chofetz Chaim said dybbukim would stop, so that emunah remains a test. He links the heel to 'Hashem Elokeichem Emes' in Krias Shema, and, from the Divrei Chaim on machine tzitzis, shows that the Satan attacks each generation's mitzvah, today emunah.

en: Chavakuk established all 613 mitzvos on emunah, and the Rav explains this as the special avodah of the last generations before Moshiach.
When following the news of the war, one must not think for a moment that a flesh-and-blood leader decides its course; the war comes only from the Ribono shel Olam.
The generations are like the limbs of Adam HaRishon; ours is the heel, which understands and feels nothing and must work and believe even in darkness.
According to the Chofetz Chaim, dybbukim ceased because in ikvesa d'Meshicha the mitzvah is pure emunah, which requires believing without seeing.
The last word of Krias Shema, 'emes', corresponds to the heel, and emes is the root of emunah.
The Satan fights the particular mitzvah each generation must strengthen; in the Divrei Chaim's time it was tzitzis, and today it is emunah.

title.en: Chavakuk's one principle and the news

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Chavakuk established the 613 mitzvos on 'tzaddik be'emunaso yichyeh' and explains it as the avodah of the last generations: emunah and hashgacha pratis. He notes that people today follow the news from Eretz Yisroel and compares it to calling the hospital every hour about a sick brother.

title.en: Not the prime minister: Hashem makes the war

summary.en: The Rav says one must not imagine that the prime minister or a general decides how the war will go; it comes only from the Ribono shel Olam. He points to the hundreds of missiles that miss or fall where they do no harm as open yad Hashem, calls the time ikvesa d'Meshicha whose mitzvah is emunah, and ends with Hashem as 'oseh chadashos, ba'al milchamos, zore'a tzedakos, matzmiach yeshuos'.

title.en: The generations as limbs of Adam HaRishon

summary.en: The Rav brings a Midrash that every soul and every generation is attached to a limb of Adam HaRishon: the generation of the desert is the head, the generation of the Beis HaMikdash the heart, and ours, ikvesa d'Meshicha, the heel, which understands and feels nothing and must only work and believe. He then begins to speak of the dybbuk known in earlier generations.

title.en: What a dybbuk is; the dybbuk in Belz

summary.en: The Rav explains that great reshaim not yet admitted to Gehinnom wander the world chased by malachei chabalah and, when a person sins, may hide inside him. He then tells how R' Yehoshua of Belz drove a dybbuk out of a girl by saying Kesser at Shabbos Mussaf.

title.en: The dybbuk in Radin

summary.en: The Rav tells the story R' Elchonon Wasserman used to repeat, also at Torah Vodaath: a girl in Radin was seized by a dybbuk, and the Chofetz Chaim sent R' Elchonon as his shliach to order it out. The dybbuk said that in heaven the Chofetz Chaim is called a Tanna, explained it entered because she drank without a brachah, and left through her small toe; the Chofetz Chaim then said there would be no more dybbukim.

title.en: Why dybbukim ended: the heel must believe

summary.en: The Rav explains the Chofetz Chaim's words: a dybbuk revealing heaven makes emunah easy, but ikvesa d'Meshicha's mitzvah is pure emunah, so dybbukim stopped. He returns to the levels of souls from head to heel and says that today the generation is the very bone of the heel, in the dark, unable to feel even what earlier generations felt at a simcha.

title.en: 'Hashem Elokeichem Emes' and the heel

summary.en: The Rav explains that Krias Shema accepts the yoke of heaven on all 248 limbs, but has 245 words, so the chazzan repeats 'Hashem Elokeichem Emes'. The last word, emes, corresponds to the heel, and emes is the root of emunah; this is why the blessings after Shema repeat 'emes', and why at night one says 'emes ve'emunah'.

title.en: Machine tzitzis and each generation's mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Divrei Chaim's teshuvah on machine matzos and machine tzitzis: machine tzitzis are pasul since they must be made lishmah, and the factory later burned down. The Divrei Chaim asked why the Satan invested so much in tzitzis and answered that each generation has its mitzvah; today it is emunah, so the Satan pours his efforts into devices that tear emunah away, and the Rav closes with Hashem as ba'al milchamos who brings yeshuos.

title.en: L'chaim and closing words

summary.en: After the shiur the recording continues with fragmentary remarks and l'chaim wishes. Most of this stretch is not transcribed and cannot be recovered.

oneLiner.en: Learning the end of Tanya chapter one, the Rav explains how the four bad middos of the animal soul come from the four elements, and why a Jew's animal soul, which comes from kelipas nogah, can be turned to holiness.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls that the animal soul lives in the blood, which is why a Jew may not eat blood, and that the sitra achra imitates holiness the way a monkey imitates a man. Everything is made of four elements, fire, air, water and earth, which he explains with everyday examples such as a balloon, water that cannot hold a shape, and gravity. From the four elements come four bad middos: anger and pride from fire, which rises; pursuit of pleasure from water; wildness, mockery and idle talk from air, which has no substance; and laziness and sadness from earth, which always falls. He then explains that a Jew's good middos and his animal soul come from kelipas nogah, the 'shining' kelipah of Yechezkel's vision, which can be raised to holiness, like orlah fruit in the fourth year and the fourth layer at a bris milah. A Jew eats with brachos and washing; even a simple Jew's good deeds are inwardly for Hashem, while a gentile's are for himself.

en: The animal soul is in the blood, so a Jew may not eat blood, since what one eats becomes part of him.
All of creation is a combination of four elements: fire, air, water and earth, corresponding to the four letters of Hashem's Name.
Four bad middos come from the four elements: anger and pride from fire, pursuit of pleasure from water, wildness and idle talk from air, laziness and sadness from earth.
A Jew's animal soul comes from kelipas nogah, which can be turned to holiness, while that of a gentile comes from the three impure kelipos, which cannot.
A gentile's good middos are ultimately for himself, while a Jew, even a simple one, inwardly does good for Hashem.

title.en: The soul in the blood and the four elements

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the animal soul is in the blood and that a Jew therefore may not eat blood, and that the sitra achra imitates holiness. He introduces the four elements that everything is made of and explains air as something real that has no substance, like the air in a balloon.

title.en: Water, earth and fire

summary.en: The Rav explains water as having substance but no stability, earth as solid, and fire as the energy in everything, including the warmth in a person. He notes that the nations call the four elements gas, liquid, solid and energy.

title.en: Anger and pride from fire, pleasures from water

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya's words that four bad middos come from the four elements in the blood. Anger comes from fire, as an angry face turns red; pride also comes from fire, because everything falls to the earth by gravity while fire alone rises. The craving for pleasures comes from water.

title.en: Wildness from air, sadness from earth

summary.en: The Rav explains that wildness, mockery, boasting and idle talk come from air, which has no substance, and illustrates with wild music that has no taste, contrasting it with real Chassidish song. Laziness and sadness come from earth, which falls fastest; a depressed person lies in bed and does not want to get up, while a joyful person rises fresh.

title.en: Kelipas nogah and the fourth year of orlah

summary.en: The Rav explains that even the natural good middos of Jews, mercy and kindness, come from kelipas nogah, the weakest kelipah, which can go either to holiness or to impurity. He brings Yechezkel's vision of four barriers, the last being nogah, like a window shade the sun shines through, and the mitzvah of orlah: three years forbidden, the fourth year holy.

title.en: How a Jew eats

summary.en: The Rav contrasts a rich gentile who eats breakfast in bed out of desire with an honest Jew, who first washes, says Modeh Ani, puts on tefillin and davens, then washes for bread and makes hamotzi. Through this the Jew turns his eating into holiness, which is possible because his animal soul comes from kelipas nogah.

title.en: Bris milah and doing good for Hashem

summary.en: The Rav compares the bris milah, where three layers are cut off and the fourth is raised through priah, to the four kelipos. He concludes that a gentile's good middos, even mercy, are for himself, while a Jew, even a simple one, inwardly does everything for Hashem, and a finer Jew eats in order to serve Hashem.

oneLiner.en: At a l'chaim, the Rav says that in a troubled time Jews need rachamim, and that even after open miracles and a Divine promise one must still daven, so perhaps one should not be so quick to skip Tachanun.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that the Jews, and the whole world, need rachamim (Divine mercy) now: things are boiling, and in September a separate state is to be declared, and no one knows what will come of it. He recalls that during the first intifada a rav arranged in his community that Avinu Malkeinu and V'hu Rachum be said every day. He then describes recent open miracles, such as a rocket that fell and did not explode while the other side wonders why; elsewhere such attacks cause great loss. Yet knowing that Hashem makes miracles does not exempt one from davening: Eliyahu HaNavi was told it would rain after three years of drought, and still he davened for it. The Rav therefore suggests that perhaps one should not be so liberal about omitting Tachanun for yahrtzeits that do not truly concern us, especially on Monday and Thursday.

en: The Rav says that the Jews and the whole world now need rachamim, since the situation is tense and no one knows what will come.
Hashem has shown great miracles, such as a rocket that did not explode, but knowing that miracles happen does not replace tefillah.
Eliyahu HaNavi davened for rain even after he was told that it would rain.
The Rav suggests that perhaps one should not be so liberal about skipping Tachanun for yahrtzeits that do not truly concern us, especially on Monday and Thursday.

title.en: Rachamim, miracles and Tachanun

summary.en: The Rav says the world needs rachamim in a tense time, tells of recent open miracles, and brings Eliyahu HaNavi, who davened for rain even after being promised it, to suggest that one should not be quick to skip Tachanun.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that on Rosh Hashanah, through the shofar and the pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, Klal Yisrael draws down the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy and creates a new world, as Hashem saved Noach out of love, and that the day is to be met with simcha and with tefillos for Klal Yisrael and the whole world.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the introduction to Zichronos, which says Hashem remembered Noach with love, and asks what love there was if the flood and Noach's survival were planned from the start. He traces the world from Adam in Gan Eden through the sin and the ten corrupt generations, and explains that Hashem planned a new world of tzaddikim to emerge from the teiva, but Cham, the dog and the raven sinned there and ruined the plan. Hashem kept Noach alive out of love, foreseeing Avraham and Klal Yisrael. That love flows from the Thirteen Attributes, which Klal Yisrael draws down with the shofar and the thirty pesukim, creating a new world as with the ten utterances. He then stresses the regular davening as the essence, tells of the Klausenberger Rebbe choosing Kriyas HaTorah over shofar, explains the Akeidah as Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael, brings the Chasam Sofer's parable on simcha in judgment, and closes with Malchus and tefillah for the world in a dangerous time.

en: Hashem kept Noach and the creatures in the teiva alive out of love even after the plan of a new world of tzaddikim was ruined, because He foresaw Avraham and Klal Yisrael.

On Rosh Hashanah Klal Yisrael creates a new world through the ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, corresponding to the ten utterances of creation, and through the shofar, which draws down the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy.
The sound of the shofar has no words; it is above speech like the utterance of Bereishis, and like the breath Hashem blew into Adam.
The regular davening is the essence of the Rosh Hashanah tefillah, and the piyutim are an addition that cannot stand without it.
The Akeidah, read on the second day, was Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael, who is called an enemy, worse than Eisav.
On Rosh Hashanah Hashem judges Jews by what they truly are in their neshamah, so the day is to be approached with simcha and confidence.
In a year of dangers for Klal Yisrael and all mankind, the Rav says the tefillos of Rosh Hashanah must be for Klal Yisrael and for the entire world.
