title.en: Why Noach was remembered with love

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Zichronos introduction praises Hashem for remembering Noach with love when the flood was planned from the start. He traces the world from Gan Eden through the sin and ten corrupt generations to the flood, and explains that a new world of tzaddikim was meant to emerge from the teiva, but Cham, the dog and the raven sinned there; Hashem saved them anyway out of love, foreseeing Avraham and Klal Yisrael.

title.en: The shofar creates a new world

summary.en: The Rav explains that Noach went out into a world that was not yet perfect, and that his survival flowed from the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, which Klal Yisrael arouses on Rosh Hashanah. With the ten pesukim of each blessing, corresponding to the ten utterances, and with the shofar, a wordless sound above speech like the utterance of Bereishis and like the breath blown into Adam, a new world is created.

title.en: The regular davening and the Klausenberger's choice

summary.en: The Rav says the regular davening, from Pesukei D'Zimra through the blessings of Krias Shema, is the essence of Rosh Hashanah and the piyutim are only an addition. He then tells how the Klausenberger Rebbe, old and weak, chose to lein the Torah rather than blow shofar, so as to arouse in Heaven Sarah's words that Yishmael must be driven out and have no share in Eretz Yisrael with Yitzchak.

title.en: The Akeidah as Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Akeidah, read on the second day, came about through Yishmael's boast to Yitzchak about his milah at thirteen, and Yitzchak's answer that he was ready to give his whole being; the Akeidah showed a mesiras nefesh Yishmael cannot match. He adds that Yishmael is called an enemy, worse than Eisav, who is only called a hater.

title.en: Simcha on the day of judgment

summary.en: The Rav explains that on Rosh Hashanah Hashem judges Jews by what they are in their neshamah, so the day is met with simcha and confidence. He brings the Chasam Sofer's parable of an imprisoned minister who rejoiced on the king's coronation day, his own day of judgment, and was pardoned and promoted, and says this joy in the King is a Jew's strength in judgment.

title.en: Accepting Malchus in a year of dangers

summary.en: The Rav says that in proclaiming Hashem's Malchus over the world one must include oneself and accept it. He describes the coming year as one of dangers for Klal Yisrael and the world, brings the passuk in Yeshayahu about Egyptian fighting Egyptian, city against city, which he connects to what is seen now, probably in Syria, and concludes that the tefillos must be for Jews and for the whole world.

title.en: Davening for the whole world

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chiddushei HaRim that Rosh Hashanah is for the entire world while Yom Kippur is between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and warns of madmen who could destroy the world. He relates a tradition from tzaddikim that before Moshiach the nations will be dragged into war against their will, and closes with a call to daven for Klal Yisrael, the world and one's family, and with the tefillah for the honor of Klal Yisrael.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Akeidah was Avraham Avinu's greatest test because Hashem seemed far away and the command clashed with His promise, and that this test of serving Hashem with joy despite unanswered questions is the test of the last generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the custom of saying the Akeidah every day and explains that a nisayon is a test that raises a person, like a pupil's exam. Avraham's first test, being thrown into the fire for a G-d who had never spoken to him, seems greater than the tenth, when Hashem commanded him directly. The Rav answers from 'he saw the place from afar': at the Akeidah Hashem felt distant, all of Avraham's levels were taken away, and he had questions, since Hashem had promised that his offspring would come through Yitzchak. Avraham went joyfully anyway, and even the simple answer, 'bring him up', was hidden from him as part of the test. Following the Ramban's principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the Rav says the last generation before Moshiach faces this same test of questions, as after the Holocaust. He closes with stories of the Lubavitcher Rebbe Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak's mesiras nefesh and defines mesiras nefesh as giving up one's will for Hashem's.

en: A nisayon is a test meant to raise a person, related to 'nes', a raised banner; each of Avraham's ten tests lifted him higher, and the Akeidah was the highest.
'He saw the place from afar' means that at the Akeidah Hashem was distant from Avraham: his lofty levels were taken from him and he felt like the simplest Jew of the generation before Moshiach.
Avraham's test at the Akeidah was having questions on Hashem, since he had been promised that his descendants would come through Yitzchak, and still going to serve Hashem with joy.
Following the principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the last generation before Moshiach faces Avraham's test of questions.
Mesiras nefesh is not only giving up one's life; giving up one's own will for Hashem's will, even once a day or once a week, adds up to great mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The Akeidah daily and what a nisayon is

summary.en: The Rav opens with the practice of saying the Akeidah every day to gain fear of Heaven, since every Jew carries something of Avraham and Yitzchak. He explains that a nisayon is a test that raises a person, like a pupil's exam, and connects it to 'nes', a raised banner; Avraham's ten tests ran from Ur Kasdim to the Akeidah.

title.en: The first test against the tenth

summary.en: The Rav tells how Avraham reasoned his way to the Creator, defied Nimrod, was thrown into the fire and saved, and only then received his first prophecy. He asks why that first test, for a G-d who had never spoken to him, should be smaller than the Akeidah, which Hashem commanded him directly in prophecy.

title.en: He saw the place from afar

summary.en: The Rav answers from 'he saw the place from afar': 'the place' is Hashem, and He was distant. With the example of a bachur who one morning learns and davens with feeling and another day cannot, he explains greater and lesser states of mind, and says that at the Akeidah all of Avraham's levels were taken from him.

title.en: The test of questions on Hashem

summary.en: The Rav says the cause of the distance was that Avraham had questions: Hashem had promised that his offspring would come from Yitzchak. A Jew with questions strengthens his emunah and does not need to understand, as when he covers his eyes for Shema; Avraham went to the Akeidah with joy. The simple answer, that Hashem only said to bring Yitzchak up, was hidden from him as part of the test.

title.en: The fathers' test as a sign for our generation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban's principle that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children, with the examples of Mitzrayim, and concludes that the last generation before Moshiach has the test of questions. He speaks of the Holocaust and the questions the heretics wrote, says that the survivors kept a stronger emunah, and that just as Avraham was blessed after the test, this generation will see great revelation. This, he says, is why the Akeidah is said every day.

title.en: The Lubavitcher Rebbe's mesiras nefesh

summary.en: Noting that tonight is the yahrzeit of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak of Lubavitch, the Rav tells of his mesiras nefesh in Russia, his answer to the interrogator's gun, and how the Stoliner Rebbe, Rabbi Yisrael, stood up for him as a young man. He then explains that mesiras nefesh, needed in the time before Moshiach, also means giving up one's will for Hashem's, and that small acts of it add up.

title.en: L'chaim and blessing

summary.en: The Rav calls for l'chaim and blesses the bachurim that Hashem help them serve Him with joy and merit the coming of Moshiach; the rest of the recording is singing and sparse, mostly untranscribed audio.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that permitted food comes from kelipas nogah and holds sparks and souls that a Jew elevates by eating it properly with a brachah, and from the Tanya's first chapter he contrasts a Jew's good middos, which can be l'shem shamayim, with the kindness of the nations, done for their own honor.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews that opposite the holiness there are four kelipos: three impure ones that cannot be transformed, and kelipas nogah, which can be turned to good. A Jew's blood and middos come from nogah, a non-Jew's from the three impure kelipos; likewise forbidden foods come from the impure kelipos and permitted foods from nogah. A Jew who eats as a Jew should, with a brachah, calmly and l'shem shamayim, elevates the food. He tells how the Yismach Moshe once ate a dish rag without noticing, explains the sparks and souls hidden in foods, why fish need no shechitah, and how thanking Hashem for the taste He gave food is itself a brachah. After a story of a young tzaddik who sold brandy, he urges bachurim to make brachos with meaning, warns about non-kosher food, and closes with the Tanya's first chapter on the source of a Jew's good middos and the self-serving kindness of the nations.

en: Opposite holiness stand three impure kelipos that cannot be transformed and kelipas nogah, which can be turned to good; a Jew's blood and middos, and all permitted food, come from nogah.
A Jew who eats as a Jew should, with a brachah, calmly and for the sake of Heaven, turns the food to good and brings it into holiness.
Every food holds sparks of holiness and parts of souls waiting for a tikun, and by hashgachah pratis each portion reaches the person whose soul is connected to it.
There are many levels of eating; the simple level is to eat l'shem shamayim in order to be healthy, without overeating, and to thank Hashem for the good taste He gave the food.
Non-kosher food becomes part of a person's body, so the Rav calls for great care in kashrus.
Following the Tanya's first chapter, a Jew's natural good middos come from the body and kelipas nogah and can be done for Hashem, while the kindness of the nations is done for themselves.

title.en: Kelipas nogah and eating like a Jew

summary.en: The Rav reviews the four kelipos: three impure ones that cannot be transformed and nogah, which can. A Jew's blood and middos and all permitted foods come from nogah, while forbidden foods come from the impure kelipos; a Jew who eats with a brachah, calmly and l'shem shamayim, elevates his food.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's supper

summary.en: The Rav says it is good to watch how a tzaddik eats, since the greatest tzaddikim do not even know when they eat. He tells how the Yismach Moshe, left to take supper alone, ate soapy dishwater with a rag in it, thinking it was meat, because his mind was on high kavanos.

title.en: Sparks and souls in food; fish and meat

summary.en: The Rav explains that since the shattering of the vessels, sparks of holiness and even souls are scattered in everything, and a brachah such as borei nefashos gives them their tikun. Souls of tzaddikim with a small blemish go into fish, so fish need no shechitah or salting, while meat needs shechitah, removal of fats and veins, and salting before only nogah remains.

title.en: Eating l'shem shamayim and the gift of taste

summary.en: The Rav says not everyone can eat like the Yismach Moshe; the simple level is eating l'shem shamayim to stay healthy, without overeating or too much sugar. Hashem could have made man run on gasoline like a car, yet He gave food taste and color, as the Rav sees in a fruit store; thanking Him for that is itself a brachah, the meaning of feeding the world with chein.

title.en: Honest eating and hashgachah pratis in food

summary.en: The Rav describes how an honest Jew eats: healthy food, a treat on Shabbos or at a simcha, a bite with coffee when weak, but not cake just because it smells good. By hashgachah pratis each portion, half an apple shared with a friend or a bottle of wine for Shabbos, holds souls connected to the one who eats it, waiting for his brachah before and after.

title.en: The brandy seller and a word to bachurim

summary.en: The Rav warns that eating without thought brings a descent instead of an ascent, and tells of a great tzaddik who as a young man sold brandy and told a customer who drank without a brachah that it was his father's yahrzeit. He then tells bachurim that they need not eat like the Yismach Moshe, but must eat like Jews: a brachah with its meaning, knowing the taste is from Hashem, and a brachah acharonah.

title.en: Non-kosher food and the kindness of the nations

summary.en: The Rav explains that non-kosher candy brings the impure kelipos into the body and becomes part of it, so in that respect it is worse even than chillul Shabbos, and kashrus needs great care. He then contrasts a non-Jew's charity, given for publicity or out of natural pity, with a Jew's, which deep in his heart is for Hashem.

title.en: Tanya chapter one: the Jew's good middos

summary.en: Reading the Tanya's first chapter, the Rav explains that a Jew's natural mercy and kindness come from the body and kelipas nogah, which is the secret of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil; he tells how Adam should have waited to make wine for kiddush. The nations' good deeds, per the Etz Chaim and the Gemara on 'chesed le'umim chatas', are done for their own honor, a fault that has crept into fundraising among Jews too.
